📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • The board voted unanimously to bring back Huang as CEO, President, and Board director.
  • Recent findings suggest that nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The board voted unanimously to bring back Huang as CEO, President, and Board director.

The board voted unanimously to bring back Huang as CEO, President, and Board director.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO. The company revealed on Monday morning that the board “voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.”.

In its statement, the board says that it received input “from senior levels of the United States government” and determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Donald Trump responded to the board’s decision in a post on Truth Social, saying Nvidia “made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO… The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”.

The board’s statement says that its investigation into reports that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot will continue, with Huang’s support and cooperation, while interim CEO Colette Kress will continue as CFO, and Harvey Jones will remain as the recently appointed board chair.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a fresh industrial revolution,” Huang said in a statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process.” This move comes after Jones said during an earnings call last week that the Nvidia board “does not intend” to return Huang as CEO.

Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month following reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees, including an executive who reported to him. In the wake of his departure, more than 200,000 people, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, signed a letter to Nvidia’s board, calling for his reinstatement.

It has been revealed that nvidia shares tumbled in Huang’s absence, while industry analysts raised concerns about an outsider replacing him at a time when Nvidia is so critical to the AI boom. Nonetheless, the board maintained as recently as last Tuesday that Huang wasn’t coming back.

Industry News: Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO of Nvidia, stock up 30%

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that nvidia has declared that disgraced CEO Jensen Huang has been reinstated to the role, effective immediately.
  • It said that the board voted unanimously in favor of reinstatement despite its recent statement that it had no intention of doing so ….
  • Sources indicate that huang’s affair with a woman suspected to be a Chinese spy became the main headline news in the tech press after coming to light at the end of last month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that nvidia has declared that disgraced CEO Jensen Huang has been reinstated to the role, effective immediately. The firm’s share price jumped more than 30% in response, with the rest of the market also making significant gains.

It said that the board voted unanimously in favor of reinstatement despite its recent statement that it had no intention of doing so ….

Sources indicate that huang’s affair with a woman suspected to be a Chinese spy became the main headline news in the tech press after coming to light at the end of last month. The Fresh York Times broke the story on October 29, citing it then as “a close relationship.” Nvidia initially denied that the relationship was anything out of the ordinary.

That changed on November 8 when Huang publicly admitted to the affair. Nvidia’s shares dropped 5%, and the firm’s board of directors opened an independent investigation. Further details emerged over the following days. Things got even worse when the same paper reported that Huang had also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

That led to Huang being fired resigning on November 12.

Despite putting the organization at enormous risk and initially lying to its board of directors, there were calls in some quarters for Huang to be reinstated. He responded by saying that he would be “honored” to return if asked to do so.

The board of directors, however, stated that it had no intention of inviting him back.

Nvidia’s chair Harvey Jones said: “The board does not intend to reinstate him.”.

That changed today, with the company making the announcement in a press release.

Industry observers note that nvidia today unveiled that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” noted Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Tech giant. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a upcoming industrial revolution,” noted Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”.

Industry observers note that as previously revealed, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.

The firm’s stock price jumped by more than 30% in response, with the rest of the market also up per Yahoo Finance.

In a recent development, nvidia shares soared more than 30% Monday morning […] The S&P 500 (^GSPC) rose 4.5% following seven straight days of declines. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) jumped more than 1,200 points to recover by 2.5% following its worst week since the COVID-related sell-off in 2020. The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) rallied 7%.

F1 in Las Vegas: You've never seen an F1 race like this before

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1884 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that las Vegas welcomed Formula 1 to its streets this past weekend.
  • The Vegas street circuit—the one that looks like an upside-down pig—is an extreme outlier on the calendar.
  • But the 17 turns are mostly all low speed, so there’s no risk of seeing the cars driving demoralizingly slowly through corners that are supposed to test one’s mettle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that las Vegas welcomed Formula 1 to its streets this past weekend. And for the first time since the event’s inception in 2023, the Grand Prix delivered on a long-promised spectacle. The racing was closer to an IndyCar oval race than anything F1 fans will have seen since slipstreaming was the order of the day at places like Monza and Hockenheim, back when humans were still landing on the Moon and downforce had yet to fundamentally change racing.

The Vegas street circuit—the one that looks like an upside-down pig—is an extreme outlier on the calendar. It has plenty of long straights, so this year’s cars still suffer from energy starvation throughout the lap, as the inadequate size of their lithium-ion hybrid batteries means they become depleted very swiftly, leaving the cars on just over half power with their V6 engines operating without the benefit of the hybrid’s electric motor.

But the 17 turns are mostly all low speed, so there’s no risk of seeing the cars driving demoralizingly slowly through corners that are supposed to test one’s mettle.

Industry observers note that and because it takes place at night, in the desert, in November, it’s cold—much, much colder than anywhere else the sport will visit all year. This coming weekend in the Middle East, track temperatures may well exceed 122° F (50° C ); on Saturday night in Nevada the track was a mere 59° F (15° C). Combined with the concrete streets, that spells low grip, but there is an added benefit—virtually no tire wear or overheating.

In a recent development, and finally, there’s the slipstream. This was far more powerful than in years past, thanks to the new aerodynamic regulations. We saw this play out in qualifying, which took place on Friday night when Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli snatched pole position by being the last man on track and benefiting from all the cars in front of him each clearing the air out of his way. Conversely, the Ferrari duo of Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc had a torrid time by not working together—a preview for the following night, as we’ll see….

Antonelli’s pole was quickly forgotten, though, as the new World Champion would only start 6th thanks to a grid penalty for using an engine component outside his allowance.

According to recent reports, because of the penalty, Red Bull’s Max Verstappen was on pole, with Mercedes’ George Russell next to him. To say there is little love lost between these two drivers would be to undersell the depths of animosity to that relationship. This was evident in FP3, when the pair clashed on track in what looked like a repeat of the Verstappen/Liam Lawson incident in Mexico. This time, no penalties were handed out.

Recent findings suggest that “He does this week in, week out with many drivers, and everybody accepts it, and I’m not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they’re bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody’s got to stand up to that guy,” Russell remarked on Friday. That set up the prospect of a lap 1, turn 1 coming together, but instead the start of the race was remarkably clean. But not boring.

Recent findings suggest that within a lap, Russell had passed Verstappen for the lead on a straight, before the Red Bull reclaimed the position going into turn 17 on the last corner. This set the tone of things to come, with the Mercedes repeatedly getting past the Red Bull at turn 14, only for Verstappen to regain the lead through sheer commitment, taking back his lead in the corners.

Don’t be tempted to call this yo-yo racing; it was nothing like the races we saw early in the season, when everyone was still trying to understand their hybrid deployment and regeneration strategies. Like an oval race, knowing when to try to move up through the pack was vital; choosing it wrong meant losing multiple positions, not just one. But like an oval, it was also possible to work one’s way up through the pack.

According to recent reports, the second Red Bull of Isack Hadjar looked more competitive than at any other time this year, and, had the two teammates worked together, they might have been able to leapfrog each other to break free of the pack—a tactic we see used to good effect on oval races. Whether Verstappen’s temperament would allow him to let his teammate past even temporarily remains unknown (I have my doubts), but Red Bull never tried it, instead ordering Hadjar to hold position, leaving him vulnerable to attack from behind. His day was ruined when his front wing exploded on lap 25, dropping him from 3rd to dead last.

So Verstappen never broke free of the chasing pack, with five or six cars covered by as little as 2.5 seconds for much of the time.

Again and again Russell took the lead briefly but lost it again to Verstappen, who worried over the radio that the Mercedes team had figured out his strategy and was going to be able to defeat it on the last lap.

According to recent reports, “I think in the beginning we had the deployment immediately correct, but of course, people are learning and watching what you’re doing. At one point, I couldn’t get back into the lead before the start-finish line, so I just—that’s why I asked the question,” Verstappen said after the race. “But I think we had it set up well, and it was just a crazy amount of fighting. The slipstream was so major that you—it was just impossible to drive off, and it was just crazy how many people were just following you.”.

But Mercedes fumbled. George Russell crashed into a barrier on lap 47—probably as he ran over a piece of Hadjar’s broken wing, preventing him from braking in time. And Antonelli blew his own chance when, instead of charging his battery for that last lap, last corner pass, he accidentally drained it entirely. The team that claimed the 2026 Constructor’s championship last time out in Mexico had to settle for another weekend off the podium.

Industry observers note that verstappen claimed his 75th win, one he remarked was more like Mario Kart than any of the previous 74. McLaren’s Lando Norris was just 0.64 seconds behind him, with the other McLaren of Oscar Piastri a similar gap behind his teammate. The orange pair worked well together and took home a massive bounty of points in their fight with Ferrari for second place in the constructor’s championship as a result.

In a recent development, ferrari’s Friday was already being called a disaster, as the two red cars couldn’t make it into the third and final qualifying session. Had they worked together to tow each other, this might have been possible. But things are far from harmonious at Ferrari between their two very closely matched drivers, with plenty of fireworks recently in Mexico City.

Industry observers note that during the race things got worse. The cars stratified themselves according to performance, which meant teammates running together often. Early on, Hamilton and Leclerc kept it mostly clean, although Hamilton earned a 10-second penalty when he went off track to avoid Norris and Leclerc, dropping him to 14th at the time. With safety cars, strategy, and that strong tow, Hamilton clawed his way back up the running order and was again in front of Leclerc by lap 34.

Four laps later, Leclerc tried to pass Hamilton—despite being specifically told by his team five corners earlier to hold position. Leclerc misjudged it, like he did in Monza and Mexico, and the cars made contact, dropping Hamilton to 10th. The race stewards clearly apportioned blame to Leclerc, handing him a 10 second penalty. Hamilton eventually finished 7th, Leclerc 10th.

Leclerc appears desperate to show the team he’s better than the seven-time champion it hired to race alongside him, but time and again his efforts end badly, costing the team points instead. Team boss Fred Vasseur had evidently read Leclerc part one of the riot act before the media pen—the palid, tear-stained face of the Mongasque driver was that of a man who looked like he knew he really screwed up this time. Having signed a massive multiyear contract, his position with the team is presumably safe. But were I Vasseur, one of Ferrari’s reserve drivers would be getting a call to get ready to replace him for the weekend in Qatar.

Like Leclerc and Hamilton, Russell has been writing checks about Verstappen his racing hasn’t cashed, and in the post-race interview, Verstappen had simply epic levels of disrespect for the other driver.

“The thing is, he speaks a lot next to the track, and honestly, you know, for me, it doesn’t really bother me because he’s so far below my level that it doesn’t really make any sense for me anyway to try and challenge that, you know? So it doesn’t bother me,” Verstappen noted. “And today, karma is a bitch. It was honestly fantastic when I looked in my mirror and I saw what was happening, so I was like, “Fantastic, my day is only getting better.” And of course, when I then crossed the line in first, my day was complete.”.

Recent findings suggest that so many unique circumstances went into making this particular Las Vegas Grand Prix as exciting as it was, and there’s little chance the next two rounds, which both take place in the Middle East, will see similar conditions. But F1 can take something away from this race to make future seasons better, and it’s to do with the tires.

It all goes back to the 2010 Canadian Grand Prix. Like this year in Vegas, Canada 2010 was chaotic. The weather was cold, the traction zones were covered in a low-grip surface to combat the tarmac disintegration seen the years before, and the action was unpredictable as each team tried to figure out on the fly how best to adapt.

F1’s powers that be saw this, and when they awarded Pirelli a sole supplier contract for tires the following year, they instructed the manufacturer to make race tires that would cause the same effect. Of course, it hasn’t ever worked out like that. Canada 2010 was a one-off and caught the teams off guard. But running the same Pirelli tires race after race, everyone swiftly figured out the optimal strategy, leaving little room for chaos.

And the Pirelli tires, while better than they once were, are still difficult to drive on. Pirelli mandates high minimum pressures out of fear of tire failures and next week in Qatar has told teams they cannot run a set for more than 27 laps. And as we frequently see in races, tires that stay within their temperature window while running in clean air can quickly overheat when following behind another car. In the wake of a car ahead, the following car has less downforce and will slide more in the corners, which puts more heat into the tires, and the trailing car falls behind instead. Pirelli makes the tires that F1 asks for, but after this weekend’s race, it’s time for the sport to ask for something different.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The enhancement swaps blocky wireframes for a photorealistic overhead feed and promises a “25x” safety boost, even as federal regulators continue investigating the software.﻿.

The update swaps blocky wireframes for a photorealistic overhead feed and promises a “25x” safety boost, even as federal regulators continue investigating the software.﻿.

Tesla has begun rolling out Full Self-Driving (Supervised) v15, calling it a ground-up overhaul of its end-to-end driver assist system. The centerpiece is Reality View, a real-time generative display that swaps out old wireframe graphics for a live, overhead camera angle that lets drivers see and tap to influence what the car plans to do next.

The third-person perspective renders buildings, crosswalks, pedestrians, and surrounding traffic with a photorealism that has drawn immediate comparisons to Grand Theft Auto VI (which conveniently debuted just days earlier). Even Elon Musk couldn’t resist the comparison on X, posting “FSD is GTA irl” shortly after the revision dropped on Saturday.

Under the hood, FSD v15 runs on an upgraded vision encoder shared across Tesla’s FSD, Robotaxi, and Optimus humanoid robot programs. By training the model on millions of online videos, Tesla claims its AI learned to prevent serious driving mistakes 25 times more often while using less computing power. Of course, the update is built for vehicles running Tesla’s newer AI4 (HW4) hardware and upcoming Cybercab platforms, leaving millions of older HW3-equipped cars behind.

Beyond the flashy visuals, v15 packs several practical upgrades. A new Bike Rack Mode lets drivers engage FSD even with hitch accessories attached (though it disables reversing, Summon, and Autopark). The system can now automatically ease off the speed near traffic cameras, with an option to override and permanently mute specific cameras after two cancellations. Tesla also promises sharper hazard avoidance for potholes, standing water, and small animals, alongside smoother speed handling in school zones and bad weather.

In a recent development, meanwhile, navigation learns preferred neighborhood routes and favorite parking spots over time, and the cabin camera can now track driver attention through hats and sunglasses while dialing back nagging alerts at higher speeds. Tesla has a pretty poor reputation for ensuring its drivers stay alert while using FSD, so hopefully this upgrade can improve that.

Still, Reality View raises an obvious question: is a hyper-detailed, video-game-style feed on the center touchscreen a helpful window into the car’s “brain,” or a tempting latest distraction? For drivers who find the live feed overwhelming, Tesla includes a map-only option and a stripped-back “quiet mode”.

Sources indicate that tesla’s bold “25x” safety claim also lands amid intense federal scrutiny. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is actively investigating roughly 2.9 million FSD-equipped vehicles over reports of Teslas blowing through red lights, crossing railroad tracks improperly, and driving into oncoming lanes. Alongside dozens of cumulative fatalities linked to Tesla’s driver-assistance systems since 2019, the probe is a stark reminder of the gap between Tesla’s autonomous ambitions and a system that still legally requires a human to keep their eyes on the road.

Nvidia on Monday announced Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO, effective immediately, a dramatic twist in a scandal that hammered the chipmaker's stock price and rocked the tech and artificial intelligence industries.

Recent findings suggest that the board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him. The board added that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and that it is confident Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk.".

President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had been speaking to Nvidia's board "directly and indirectly," and that Huang "did nothing wrong." Trump said he talked to Huang on Sunday and asked him to promise to "work hard.".

Huang resigned from his role as chief executive earlier this month after a series of shocking reports about multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The New York Times reported on Sunday that the woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer at China's Ministry of State Security during at least part of the time that she was engaging in a relationship with Huang.

Shares of Nvidia surged 33% following Huang's reinstatement. The stock had shed nearly 33% from the time Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on Nov. 8.

"I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a latest industrial revolution," Huang remarked in a statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process.".

In a recent development, senior government officials briefed Nvidia's board late last week and communicated that no national security laws were violated, according to sources familiar with the discussion who asked to remain anonymous because they were not authorized to speak publicly. That upgrade prompted the board to reach out to Huang, the people remarked.

Huang and the board held their first conversations since his ouster on Saturday, and the group determined he would return as CEO during a second meeting on Sunday, the people said. Nvidia's cratering stock price played a role in accelerating those conversations.

Recent findings suggest that trump celebrated Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday, writing in a post on his social media site that the board made "the correct and proper decision" to reinstate him. Trump stated the U.S. needs Huang's leadership to "ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Organization, but the American Economy.".

He reiterated that the U.S. government has "no reason to believe" that Huang's return poses a risk to national security, and that it "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.".

"On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure," Trump wrote.

Recent findings suggest that several tech industry leaders, including Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, Gavin Baker, managing partner and CIO at Atreides Management, and Brad Gerstner, Altimeter Capital CEO, had been actively lobbying for Huang's return. Musk wrote in a post on X on Monday that the board's "mistake has been corrected.".

Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

Industry observers note that for weeks following Huang's ouster, the firm's board maintained that it was not considering Huang's reinstatement. It appointed Colette Kress, Nvidia's CFO, as the chipmaker's interim CEO, who reiterated that position in an interview with CNBC following Huang's exit. Kress will continue to serve as Nvidia's CFO, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Sources indicate that nvidia's board formed an independent committee and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an investigation into Huang and whether company secrets or national security were compromised. The board stated Monday that "the committee's investigation will proceed to conclusion" and that Huang is "committed to cooperating with it.".

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia Board Chair Harvey Jones said in a statement. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Manufacturer.

Even with Huang back at the helm, Nvidia is facing increased scrutiny over its chip sales to Southeast Asia and China.

Lawmakers have been preparing for investigations into how Huang's affair with the alleged spy may have damaged U.S. AI dominance, influenced his positions on export controls and impacted his close relationships with Trump and his Cabinet. Huang has been one of the loudest voices opposing strict export controls on advanced chips.

According to recent reports, "The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the organization's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., mentioned in a statement on Monday.

Industry observers note that huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels on Dec. 2. Those dates were set prior to Huang's return, and John Fisher, who represents Huang, did not comment on whether there are any chances in his looks to testify.

Sources indicate that "Americans deserve answers about what NVIDIA and the Trump administration knew, when they knew it, and whether sufficient steps were taken to prevent sensitive technology from falling into the wrong hands," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., wrote in a post on X on Monday.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In its latest salvo against New York City's Delivery Protection Act, Amazon is trying to win over residents with a new tactic.
  • After introducing notifications on its mobile app warning of potential extra fees, the company has now started attaching stickers to packages with with similar warnings of increased prices The message includes a QR code that would allow customers to contact their representative and protest the changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The company claims the changes could add ‘up to $5 per order.’.

In its latest salvo against New York City's Delivery Protection Act, Amazon is trying to win over residents with a new tactic. The manufacturer has started applying stickers to packages threatening that changes to last-mile deliveries proposed by NYC council could add "up to $5 per order," according to The Verge and multiple Reddit posts.

After introducing notifications on its mobile app warning of potential extra fees, the company has now started attaching stickers to packages with with similar warnings of increased prices The message includes a QR code that would allow customers to contact their representative and protest the changes.

It has been revealed that in August, Fresh York City mayor Zohran Mamdani declared that he was backing the Delivery Protection Act (Intro 518), announced several months prior. Companies that do high-volume deliveries, particularly Amazon, rely on contractors rather than employees to take packages on the final legs of their journeys to customers. The proposed legislation would create new licensing rules for those last-mile operations as well as requiring the delivery workers to be manufacturer employees rather than contractors.

The Teamsters union and other supporters of the bill have argued that it will hold corporations like Amazon responsible for deliveries while offering better pay and benefits to the professionals making those deliveries. However, Amazon has stated the bill would lead to increased costs and slower deliveries for customers. It also threatened to move its distribution centers out of New York City to avoid the regulation.

Given Mamdani's popularity and the average American's hatred of large tech companies, Amazon's latest gambit may be unwise and ill-fated. "Latest Yorkers support this law. Amazon's propaganda machine is trying to make us think otherwise," Redditor u/SkippyReddit wrote.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Journalist Darryl Campbell breaks down the mundane management failures behind the FAA’s nationwide meltdown, and what it will take to fix a system held together with duct tape.

Today I’m talking with Darryl Campbell, a freelance journalist, aviation expert, and author of the book Fatal Abstraction: Why the Managerial Class Loses Control of Software.

In a recent development, darryl covers aviation and the FAA, and earlier this month, when the US suffered a sudden nationwide ground stop on air travel, Darryl was all over the story. He published a great report for us on The Verge about what happened, what and who was to blame, and what we might do about the underlying infrastructure failures in the aviation business.

So ahead of Thanksgiving, one of the country’s major holiday travel weeks, I wanted to have Darryl on the show to walk us through this incident on Friday, November 13th, when the FAA grounded every departing flight in the country for more than four hours.

In a recent development, you’ll hear us work backward from how a single router could cause this kind of damage to why our aviation infrastructure is so painfully out of date and what the government plans to do about it. Also, why incidents like this are creating a kind of swirling paranoia about AI and cyberattacks, even when the real culprit is far more mundane.

In a recent development, okay: aviation journalist Darryl Campbell on the FAA ground stop. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Darryl Campbell, you’re a journalist, you’re an aviation expert, and you’re the author of the book Fatal Abstraction: Why the Managerial Class Loses Control of Software, which is potentially the most Decoder title in all of publishing history. Welcome to Decoder.

Thanks very much. Longtime listener, first-time caller. So thanks for having me.

According to recent reports, I love that book title. I love all the ideas that it suggests. We’ll have you back to talk about the book, but I feel like we’re going to use that idea to talk about air traffic control today on Decoder with you.

Yeah, I think so much of what we’ve found out, even in the week since my report came out, has really just been a lot of boring management failures that have somehow cascaded to affect millions of people on thousands of flights. And it’s just the importance of actually having people who know what they’re doing in charge.

Industry observers note that there’s a lot there already. There’s a whole hour of Decoder right there. But what you’re referencing is the fact that you wrote a story for us about the nationwide ground stop the FAA had to call because of a bad router. Tell us what we know. What happened here? Why did air traffic control ground you all?

I’m going to take you back to Friday the 13th in a part of the country that nobody really associates with aviation, which is a little place called El Dorado, Arkansas. It’s the very tail end of part of this significant backbone of data and telecommunications that’s really a private network run exclusively for air traffic control by a firm called L3Harris, who runs it on behalf of the FAA.

They’re just going in there, and they’re replacing what is essentially like 50-year-old infrastructure. If you remember back in the ‘90s, early 2000s when you made your first switch from DSL to fiber optic, that is exactly what they’re trying to do there, except-.

So just to remind everybody, DSL ran on the phone lines.

Yeah, so this is like a cable modem. So I’m old enough to remember that, and maybe some of you out there are. But yeah, this is like as soon as you plug in fiber, your speeds get five to 10 times faster. And that sounds great, but in the private telecom world, that happens on entirely separate networks.

Your DSL provider isn’t your fiber provider, or if they are, they’re running on parallel networks. The FAA system has to do both at the same time, and so you have to figure out how we get all of these different cables, different routers, different protocols for how these things transmit data to all play nice with the same reliability and uptime? Because you need that when you’re managing tens of thousands of flights every single day.

One of the things that I think is really important to understand here is that the FAA runs its own private network. It’s called the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure. It was built by this contractor back in the ‘90s and early 2000s. So it’s old, and it is actually due to be replaced, correct?

According to recent reports, yeah, and that’s part of the challenge, because you have to have it to keep the aviation system going; you can’t just shut it down for a week, rip everything out, and replace it. So they’ve been doing piecemeal upgrades over time, and a lot of it is done by this L3Harris contractor, who’s one of the biggest defense companies in the world. They’ve been working with the FAA for a long time. You would think that they would know how to do a simple router swap without causing everything to go down, but that’s exactly what happened on Friday.

If you go back and look at everything that exactly caused the outage, it’s like a comedy of errors. No single thing would have caused the entire system to crash, but every little missed opportunity, failed connection, or decision that somebody made with no knowledge of what happens downstream from everything, really led to the point where all of a sudden the most congested airspace in the world could not figure out where the airplanes were. They couldn’t talk to people who are en route, and that’s a serious safety problem that could have put thousands of people at risk.

Let’s work backwards from the actual precipitating incident, and then let’s talk about the government’s response to this crisis. So there’s a router swap that happens in Arkansas. In your story, you say they swapped in a fiber router for an old copper router, and that thing started sending out too many requests for the network it was connected to.

So L3Harris is trying to replace what is essentially a telephone switch from the 1960s with a new modern fiber optic data router. And so they’re removing the cabling, they’re removing the switch, and replacing it.

Recent findings suggest that now, if you’re on, let’s say, a perfectly modern networking system, and you’re switching out a fiber optic for a fiber optic line, the data routing is the same; the protocols that the routers use to communicate with each other are the same. Do you remember that DSL to fiber optic comparison we made? That’s not really an problem because everything can handle huge amounts of data with high throughput.

When the manufacturer sends out these fresh routers, there’s a factory setting on it that says, “Okay, when you’re making a communication attempt for the first time, assume that you are doing it with a high-throughput fiber optic system.” L3Harris forgot to turn off that switch, and so as soon as they plug in-.

Yeah, from what I can tell and from all the reports that have come out, that is literally it. So L3Harris has stated, “Hey, we did what we were supposed to. The router manufacturer said everything was working as it’s supposed to. There was no problem with the machine. It’s just that someone forgot to say, ‘Hey, you’re connecting to an old system.’” So when it starts pinging what it thinks is a high-capacity fiber optic data network, it’s just sending thousands and thousands of communication requests.

According to recent reports, now, on their own, and if this wasn’t a critical infrastructural system, it probably would have done what I compare to a FaceTime call with bad Wi-Fi. All these connection requests start displacing some of the normal data packets that come through the network, and you start losing a couple of data packets, and so maybe the image quality degrades, or the audio starts to skip or something like that. That’s fine if you’re just trying to talk to someone in a normal one-on-one setting.

It has been revealed that but again, this is the air traffic control system for the world’s largest air traffic network, and you really can’t have any kind of data lag. And so what pilots start to see is the air traffic control routing centers that handle the high-altitude airplanes, the ones who are in cruise control and whatever; first, they start seeing some transmission loss. Sometimes it’s a radio transmission that cuts out. Over time, it gets worse as this router keeps pinging the system and keeps blasting it with all of these connection requests that cause data loss.

And then that starts cascading. So it’s not just radio traffic. It then becomes radar data, too, and then it becomes so overwhelming that entire centers are going offline. At the peak of the crisis, when Secretary Sean Duffy decided to start this ground stop, 17 out of the 22 en route control centers around the country had gone dark, and they were unable to communicate with airplanes that were en route, or see where they were, without having to rely on a backup system.

Sources indicate that that strikes me as all very bad, and as we saw, there was a ground stop. Why did it take quite as long as it did for anyone to say what happened?

Industry observers note that I’m thinking about [Transportation Secretary] Sean Duffy and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and their, frankly, absurd press conferences where they were saying conflicting things back to back from one another. They were not ruling out cyber attacks. What happened there? Why did it take so long to come up with what seems like a simple explanation for a very complicated problem?

Sources indicate that yeah, well, if it sounded like people didn’t know what they were talking about, it’s because they didn’t. If you remember back in, I think, February of 2025, Elon Musk going in there with DOGE and firing a couple hundred people at the FAA. Now, you remember at the time — and in fact, I wrote a piece about it for The Verge — they said, “These aren’t safety-critical people. These aren’t the radar technicians. They’re not air traffic controllers.” That was true. But what they were was network engineers, data technicians, telecom specialists. These are the people who would have been overseeing the work that L3Harris was doing, and they simply did not exist.

Industry observers note that so there was a CNN report that came out about this trail of evidence, where usually what would happen is the contractor comes in with a router, and then an FAA technician meets them and oversees the work. They do some tests to make sure that everything is going okay and that nothing is going to disrupt the entire system. Everybody signs off, and then everyone goes home, and nobody really knows that anything happened.

Well, guess what didn’t happen? The FAA technician did meet the contractor, but they didn’t oversee any of the work. The contractor didn’t say that they were done. They didn’t let the FAA know that they were going to start testing. All of these decisions and all of these theoretically simple, easy tasks related to basic good management and governance didn’t happen. By the time people figured out what was going on, we were already four hours into what was the worst ground stop since 9/11.

How did we figure out what was going on?

It has been revealed that so eventually L3Harris started isolating parts of the data management system — basically taking routers offline. That’s why one of the initial reports came out and stated, “Oh, we think we’ve isolated the problem to a part of the country that spans Arkansas and Texas.” And then, just one by one, taking these routers dark, they eventually turned off the single router that had gone and started creating these connection requests.

Industry observers note that once that was offline, which honestly took them until around 7:40PM or 8PM ET on Friday, they were able, almost instantaneously, to start getting data and radar connections back. And then they decided to release the ground stop at that point. But it was really just your classic IT debugging of turning things off and seeing if anything changed until they found the right one.

Sources indicate that that’s right. Turn it off, turn it back on again.

Recent findings suggest that I stated I wanted to move backwards. You stepped back to DOGE. Elon Musk comes in with DOGE. He takes the chainsaw to bureaucracy. He fires a bunch of network technicians. It seems like a bunch of processes go out the window. But this is a long story, right? This is a rickety system that we’ve known needed to be upgraded for years. Is it really just DOGE that brought us to the brink of incompetence, or is there a story beyond that?

Yeah, I think it’s not just years, but decades. I mean, the main problem is that the money, effort, and sustained attention required to do all of these kinds of boring network upgrades operate on time horizons that are like five to 10 years. Whereas in politics, your time horizon is maybe a year or two max, every time you’re going back to budgeting, to getting the political will to get things passed.

Because those things are so far out of sync, number one, it’s hard to just get the money in the first place to do these expensive upgrades. Number two, keep the money going so that the project is perfectly budgeted and the contractors have started on it, then get the money to keep doing the work that they need to do for a couple of years. And then number three, to maintain that momentum across administrations, across congressional changes, and really across party shifts. That’s been the big problem — that whenever a sort of smaller government, anti-regulation administration comes in, they start cutting some of the funding, and usually the FAA is on the chopping block.

It’s almost kind of ironic that pilots, air traffic controllers, and the people who operate the system behind the scenes have actually gotten so good at making up for the FAA and the air traffic control system’s flaws — just because their machines are literally falling apart — that we’ve kind of papered over some of the issues and gone around some of the problems. If these had surfaced maybe five or 10 years ago, maybe we would be a little bit faster about getting the upgrades that we need today.

It has been revealed that just continuing the theme of moving backwards, it’s not as though people didn’t know, right? There was funding to modernize the system. That funding was controversial in the way that whenever Democrats pass funding and Republicans take power, the funding becomes controversial.

It’s funny. There’s a video of Sec. Duffy saying the Biden administration was wasting money that they should have been spending on the FAA. And then after this incident, he’s begging for $50 billion at a press conference. It seems like everyone knew about the problem, right? We have a proposal to fix it. There’s a date to replace the system. Why isn’t there more urgency?

Yeah, so I think there are two parts to your question here. I think number one is the political will required to get the budget in the first place, which is kind of like a two- to three-year process where you have to identify the company that can actually do the work. That’s part of the reason why we’ve got all these substantial incumbent defense companies because you can’t have some startup in San Francisco figure out how to change 3,000 miles of cabling overnight. That just can’t be done.

And then you have to go through the work of getting it passed through Congress, through all of the accountability layers like the Government Accountability Office and all of the other procedural guardrails that are designed to keep government waste somewhat under control. That’s largely good, except that by the time we get the reports and actually figure out, okay, here’s what we need to do, here’s the right vendor, and so on, usually that’s after a midterm or after an administration change, and the political will has already kind of gone out the window.

So I think that’s one part of it. And I think the second part is the FAA is just kind of suffering from death by a thousand cuts over the last 20, 30, 40 years. Even if they do the right thing, which is that they should be replacing a lot of these older switches with upcoming routers, by the time that happens, all of the other complications with the administration and the agency have kind of filtered down to the point where they just don’t have the people in place.

Let’s say you’re a network engineer who really knows their stuff and who could be in the right place for it. After three to five years of just sort of will they, won’t they, am I going to have a job next year, and all of the other things that get in the way of you being able to do your job, you’re probably going to go into private industry at that point. So I think there’s a talent problem and there’s this kind of overall political problem that’s really causing a lot of these concerns.

Recent findings suggest that I want to rewind to the beginning of the second Trump administration, which feels like 10 million years ago, but it was not so long ago. It was two years ago. Elon comes in with DOGE; he’s got the chainsaw for bureaucracy, and he’s firing these people. He’s maybe getting rid of some of the talent you’re talking about.

But there’s also a bunch of aviation catastrophes that happened, right? Planes were crashing, there were near misses at airports, and we heard a lot about how, because Elon was in the government, we would instantly modernize our infrastructure. We were going to rip Verizon out and replace it with Starlink. We were going to AI vibe code all the software. Did anything come of that, or did anything happen because of that?

A couple of things have happened, but not to the extent that they’re addressing some of the major problems with the system. I think the biggest challenge here, and it’s kind of a quirk of the U.S. air traffic control system, is that our regulator and also the entity that operates all of the infrastructure and air traffic control systems are one and the same.

Recent findings suggest that it’s actually quite a hard thing for, in particular, Republicans and small government conservatives to get the idea that it’s good to fund the FAA when, in their mind, it’s a regulator as much as it is kind of the operator. That already creates a lot of challenges.

I think the second thing that we talk about, and specific to DOGE, was that a lot of the contracts that they gave out were from people in that Silicon Valley orbit. So you think about Palantir; there’s a newly introduced company called ASI that’s now running the SMART AI air traffic control system.

According to recent reports, yeah, that’s been kind of a big conspiracy theory thing. But those are great, and they’re crucial systems, but the biggest challenges for the FAA are physical in nature. How do we replace this gigantic network? How do we get these telephone switches out of the ground and replace them with fiber optics? How do we replace radar and communications technology that is, in some cases, literally held together with duct tape and aluminum foil? And that part you’re never going to be able to do as kind of a small startup operating entirely in the digital and software space.

Recent findings suggest that I mean, the people that they gave contracts to and the people that benefited the most were attacking some small part of the problem, but not the one that’s related to how do you keep airplanes from not running into each other or how do you make sure that air traffic control radios are working so that helicopters don’t crash into commercial flights. Those are really hard, intractable, physical world problems that this sort of Silicon Valley AI vibe coding thing is never going to solve.

Recent findings suggest that there was some amount of drama about Verizon being ripped out and replaced with Starlink. The idea that we could just upgrade the networks and equip all the planes with latest sensors — there was energy around that in the beginning of the Trump administration. It appears to have just completely fizzled.

It has been revealed that it’s part of this contractual incumbent thing. You can say whatever you want about replacing a vendor you don’t like with the one from your buddy down the hall, but it’s going to take years. Verizon, I think, did get moved out of some contracts, but they were replaced with another big telecom tech giant, not Starlink.

I mean, I’m pretty sure that there’s one Starlink system, and it’s operating in the middle of nowhere in Alaska. So on paper, yeah, Starlink has something, but again, they’re just not equipped to handle some of the big problems with all of this sort of legacy cabling and networking.

According to recent reports, you mentioned your buddy’s tech giant down the hall. That brings us directly to ASI, which is the center of one of the hottest conspiracy theories about the ground stop that exists. Sean Duffy’s son, Michael Alfonso, is running for office. ASI contributed to his campaign.

People have drawn this connection. They think there’s some sort of kickback, but ASI was hired to implement some AI-based system, or SMART system, that was going on while the ground stop happened. Are these things connected in any way?

According to recent reports, in a word, no. A lot of the conspiracy theories that have come up around this SMART system really came about in this gray space because the messaging from the administration was so bad, and there’s this natural antipathy towards AI. But all that SMART is doing is replacing some of the manual printouts and the routing that happens at the level of air traffic controllers in sort of control towers and facilities.

It has been revealed that they’re not actually plugged into the data backbone. They’re not handling any of the radar or the sensitive radio data. They’re just kind of a parallel system operating out in space. Now that being said, it’s because you’ve got the Secretary of Transportation and the Secretary of Homeland Security out there kind of shooting from the hip at their press conference that inspired exactly zero confidence in the messaging that they were giving.

Industry observers note that to give him a little bit of credit, Sean Duffy did say a couple of accurate things, but the way that he noted them and then literally in the next sentence walked it back and said, “But it could be 10 other things,” does not inspire confidence at all. I think networking is a hard thing to explain to your average person because their eyes may glaze over, and then you have someone who really doesn’t understand it, who’s trying to do the right thing. But in his mind, the main point of that whole press conference was to get to that $30 or $50 billion shakedown of the government. So he’s kind of blowing past the technical details in the first place.

It was just not a great look, and I think that’s why some of this conspiracy theory stuff has started to thrive.

Industry observers note that you mentioned the natural antipathy towards AI. Obviously, this ground stop happened in the context of many other outages. Microsoft Outlook went down. United had an problem that brought it down for several hours. There were other outages this week. There was a Chase Bank outage that people overread into thinking it was a banking system outage.

In a recent development, there’s a lot of AI antipathy out there. There’s a lot of, “Well, this must be either AI-powered cyber attacks or everyone’s vibe coding garbage software and pushing into production; it’s crashing.” The top comment on your story is, “I call BS on this. It was AI, but we won’t hear it. They’re using this to beg for money they need after Elon Musk tore air traffic control apart.” Is there an AI element to this story at all?

I would say to that commentary that it gets two out of the three, so that’s pretty good. The AI component, I think, is really more about what happens in three to five years when we fully transition, I’m sure, to this AI-powered system. I think that’s the part where we’re really going to see how good it is.

Right now, air traffic controllers are still using legacy processes to route planes and keep track of everything. And those processes work pretty well. I mean, I’ve talked with hundreds of air traffic controllers over the years. They’re uniformly professional, very skilled, and more importantly, they know the ways that their systems will break down so that when something happens, they can immediately figure out how to keep things going without putting everybody at risk.

When you do eventually move to the SMART AI system, that’s going to be a whole unknown. And I think that’s really kind of where my concern would be: when they turn it on for a larger portion of the air traffic control system, where they say, “Okay, from now on,” I’m just making this up, “Chicago is going to be on the SMART system, and we’ll see what happens.” That’s the day that maybe I would avoid flying for a little while.

According to recent reports, I don’t have the data to back this up, but it just feels like flying has gotten more chaotic and dangerous in the second Trump administration than before. There have been more crashes. Is that related to management incompetence? Is that just a string of bad luck?

It has been revealed that chaotic for sure. I think dangerous, probably not. I mean, if you think about the incentives that line up, airlines do not want to have a crash. Passengers don’t want to fly on something dangerous. So with whatever’s going on at the administration level, there’s enough pushback within industry and within the passenger market that nobody is really going to take steps that they think will actively degrade the system.

Recent findings suggest that that being mentioned, I would say you’re 100 percent justified in thinking that you should be less confident in the regulation and operations leadership side today than you would be five years ago. You heard it on Friday night and Saturday morning that the people in charge don’t really care what’s going on, and they just want the optics to look good. Even if you push them on the details, the people who knew what they were doing are really not in place anymore. I think we’ll probably see more of these disruptions over the next couple of years. I don’t think we’ll ever see anything that gets to the point of being materially more unsafe.

In large part, I think the ground stop was probably justified. I mean, I talked to a bunch of controllers who mentioned, “We could have handled it. We could have gone to backup systems, and in 20, 30, 40 minutes, things would’ve been more or less back to normal.” And I believe them. I think they absolutely could have handled some of these outages without causing any real safety risks.

Recent findings suggest that but from a passenger standpoint, you also don’t want to hear, and that’s part of the reason I started the story with that anecdote, “Hey, this is your pilot. We can’t communicate with anybody. We’re going to kind of see how it goes.” That is a very scary thing to hear.

According to recent reports, I think that really fuels a lot of it: that any kind of perceived safety risk in aviation just awakens this primordial fear in people. That’s totally justified. And I think it helps keep some of these anti-regulation impulses in check because people know that once a critical mass of people are afraid of flying, you kind of undo an industry that holds the entire United States and, in many respects, the world together.

One of the things that’s really interesting about this dynamic, this whole story, is that if you were to design an air traffic control system from scratch today, it would be vastly more automated, right?

You would absolutely have an enormous amount of computer control over where the airplanes are. You would build vastly more powerful communication between planes and air traffic control centers in between them, and you would maybe even just let ATC control the planes directly, right?

According to recent reports, it’s a closed ecosystem where everyone wants to participate and has aligned incentives. You would just say, “Okay, the robots are going to fly all the planes for us, and they’re going to be perfectly safe.” But it doesn’t seem like there’s a pathway from here to there.

At least not in the United States. I think there are so many counterarguments to some of the good intentions that people have, and frankly, a lot of people are just trying to get in because they want a hand of the government payout pie. I would be very worried if someone noted, “Hey, tomorrow we’re going to launch robot planes coming out of Atlanta.”.

I do think a potential competing model is what we see in China, where they don’t have some of these competing economic or political gamesmanship kind of counterforces going on, where they are able to build what is essentially a newly introduced air traffic control system largely from scratch and with updated technology. And I think we are seeing some of the ways that automation is making that more efficient.

Sources indicate that that being said, I would bet you $100 that would never happen in the US, at least not until something materially changes in the way that the US thinks about air travel. I mean, we think about it as a right. We think about it as the primary way that we get from point A to point B other than driving a car for 100 miles, and we think about it as something that everybody should have access to.

So, that means we want it cheap, we want it fast, and we’re kind of able to tolerate some of these large-scale disruptions as long as it doesn’t affect our Thanksgiving looks in a week. I think that also just kind of keeps the system the way it is in ways that maybe are not the case in some other countries that are newer to large-scale aviation.

I like that you made reference to the cliché: you can have it cheap, fast, or good. Now pick two.

Sources indicate that that’s what you’re saying. In this case, maybe none.

There’s another argument I’ve heard, and this is in Project 2025. You mentioned the industry has a lot of incentives to figure this out, to make it good, to make sure people feel safe. In Project 2025, the idea that we should privatize air traffic control exists.

Sources indicate that at the beginning of the second Trump administration, as Elon was slashing air traffic control and the FAA, the notion that this would lead inexorably to privatized air traffic control that could then impose a bunch of this stuff, because the industry would be doing it to itself, was everywhere. I heard about it constantly. That doesn’t seem to have happened. Is there a push, is there an argument to be made for private air traffic control?

We definitely saw that, and I think with Project 2025, that’s been a plank of The Heritage Foundation’s strategy for government for more than two decades, if not since the late ‘80s when Reagan fired the air traffic controllers.

According to recent reports, I think privatization is a difficult concept for a lot of people to get their head around. But I do think the core idea, which is that you kind of need to separate the FAA as regulator from FAA as air traffic control operator, is fundamentally sound, whether that means moving it into a fresh government department or some other structural change.

Industry observers note that A lot of places around the world do have privatized air traffic control, so Canada, the UK, Germany, or they have a different system entirely. In Brazil, for example, air traffic control is actually controlled by the military.

China is really the only big country that has a similar structure, but when you’re in a one-party system, it doesn’t really function as it does in the US. That is kind of a weird quirk that needs to be solved one way or another.

The quirk is that the regulator also oversees air traffic control.

Industry observers note that correct. But I just don’t know what the right pathway is because there’s also… I mean, you’re seeing it today with some of these contractors who are coming in and essentially scamming the government about everything, and that doesn’t seem to me like a safe way to operate the air traffic control system. How do you compensate for that human/corporate nature that we seem to have here, where you do kind of want to maximize profits even past the point of producing a good product?

According to recent reports, the airline industry is not full of shy characters. Ed Bastian, the CEO of Delta, is not a reserved figure. These are significant personalities; they run big businesses, they battle with each other, and they spend enormous amounts of money. As you stated, they’re the backbone of the global economy in many ways. Why can’t they push for it? Why aren’t they leading the charge?

In a recent development, ah, so there’s an interesting one. They are leading the charge publicly, while in private not really committing any considerable support to it. So let me put this in the context of aviation security. It costs the US government about $10 to screen for baggage, security, and whatever. But if you look at your airline ticket, your average FAA 9/11 fee, whatever it’s called today, is $1.50. That was because airlines pushed so hard against any kind of thing that would increase their fares that we’re essentially losing money on every security scan.

Now, whether or not security works is a whole other story, but that’s kind of the mentality that they have. It’s great for them to pontificate about what we need, but if you ask the airlines to shoulder some of the burden, they’re going to say, “Well, this is going to blow up our entire economic model.” That’s a difficult thing to swallow.

According to recent reports, I mean, in Canada, they just make them pay for the fees. The security fee is about 10 times higher. The fees for their private air traffic control system also pass through to the passengers, but that means that they don’t have your $70 “go somewhere cheap this weekend” kind of fares that we do in the US. So there are trade-offs, and I think the industry isn’t yet willing to part with some of that margin in order to upgrade the air traffic control system. They think it should be a government burden to pay.

If the listener is keeping track of us going backwards, we started with one router that was replaced with a misconfigured setting, and we’ve arrived at how we should split up the FAA and change the fee structure for airlines. That is a long and winding road, but it feels like a very direct connection.

According to recent reports, yeah, absolutely. I mean, these kinds of changes take decades to do. If you’re in that short-term mentality, that one where you’re just trying to make it to the next election or you just need this particular line on the budget, you’re never going to get to a world where we can have a fully functional air traffic system.

Part of the thing is that people do hide behind this complexity to both extract money from the government funds that are available or to just be able to… Case in point, Sec. Duffy, who, when he was a congressman, voted against funding for the FAA. Now six, seven, eight years later, he’s saying, “Oh my gosh, what a terrible idea. Whoever did that in the first place should be banned from the government. By the way, I also need $50 billion more to do it.”.

You can kind of see how short-term memory, the political cycle, and everything else line up to make sure that we kind of get the system we deserve in a way.

Let’s say Sec. Duffy was massively competent. He was the single best network design engineer that has ever existed. This is a lot for a cast member of The Real World, but so it goes. What if you gave him $50 billion? If you dumped $50 billion on the FAA today, could it accomplish building a system that was reliable, stable, much more automated, and safer?

Industry observers note that I think it could happen in a couple of years, but it’s not just the money that you would need. I think you would need a couple of other things too. Number one, you just have to have the managers who can do it. So you remember Mark Zuckerberg; his whole thing was like, “Let’s get rid of all these middle managers.” But they have a function. And especially when you’re dealing with legacy systems, complex technical installations, and the management of just large networks of people, not just data, but people.

You kind of need those people who are in these glue functions to make sure that, hey, maybe let’s not do something on a Friday afternoon when even a small failure is going to bring down a busy air traffic controller. Maybe let’s have a technician on site who knows what they’re doing and who can oversee the work. Maybe let’s have a blueprint that notes, hey, let’s check the factory settings when you plug in this thing.

It’s not just these giant top-line initiatives of a lot of money. It’s the baseline competence process and the ability to take things slowly when you need to. All of that is missing right now. If you think too hard about it, you can get really frustrated and despair about the future of air travel.

The thing that gives me confidence is that we’ve done it so far, even in these conditions where we’re not having massive numbers of crashes, and that we are willing to pause the system when it makes sense to do so. But you can only go on for so long like that.

I think this is really when we’re coming to a decision point, and at some point the equipment itself, regardless of what the politicians say, regardless of what the budget notes, the equipment itself is going to tell us, “This is unsustainable. We can’t go on anymore.” I would rather we do the work to not get to that point if we can, because I don’t want to be the person on the airplane who hears the pilot say, “Oh, we’ve lost communication with the FAA and really have no idea what’s going on.” That’s a very scary and dangerous thing to hear.

According to recent reports, we’re publishing this the Monday before Thanksgiving, which is historically one of the busiest air travel weeks of the entire year. Should people feel that the system is reliable right now?

I think we’ll get through Thanksgiving.

[Laughs] That was a long pause, dude.

Well, I was going to say that I’m staying put this Thanksgiving, so make what you will of that. I think the system, airlines, know what’s going on. Now people are on guard for that. And from what we’ve heard from the FAA, they’re not installing any new routers anytime soon. That particular risk is pretty much eliminated.

Sources indicate that I would say your safety has never really been at risk, and people are still able to manage these crises when they happen. So I wouldn’t worry about safety. I would say give yourself a couple of extra hours either way.

According to recent reports, for example, I flew to Boston over this past weekend. Saturday morning, even though the ground stop had been lifted, we were still delayed over an hour. It was not because of any communications problem, but because so many things had happened to put airplanes and people out of place that they were literally calling flight attendants on their day off to come in and work, and that’s what my aircraft was waiting for.

Recovery will happen. Disruptions can be managed to a certain extent. But I think if we get to another year from now and we’re still paralyzed in this world of, “Well, let’s just spend the time pointing fingers rather than doing anything meaningful,” then I think it really starts to call into question whether we do have the capacity to fix what’s wrong with the air traffic system.

Industry observers note that FTI, the network at issue here, is due to be replaced in 2028. Just to wrap it up, what are the markers you’re looking for to see if that process is happening as intended and we are going to wind up with a better, more reliable network?

I think by the middle of next year, we’ll be able to see the pace at which some of these projects are being implemented. And so we’ll know if there’s a problem with implementation that’s going to push out timelines for the next two to three years. I mean, the FAA has gotten really good at overpromising and underdelivering over the years. There was an entirely newly introduced air traffic control system that was supposed to be put into place between 2000 and today that just died because of a lack of political will.

One of the good things that the FAA has done is actually created a website tracking a lot of these projects. And if you’re nerdy like me, you can go on there and see, okay, this week they put a router in there in Arkansas or wherever. And so that’s really going to tell us and give us the clarity that we’ve lacked over the last couple of years: the pace of some of these projects. And to give them credit, it is creating some accountability where there wasn’t really any.

But I think it will really be monitoring over the next six to nine months to see whether this has fundamentally changed the FAA’s appetite for taking risks that will get to a better system down the road, but that may cause disruption today. And that’s really what I’d be worried about: that it’s easy and it’s practically agency policy at this point to kick the can down the road. And so if this has created so much blowback that the FAA is now completely risk-averse, there may be a world where they don’t accomplish some of these things until the 2030s.

Industry observers note that there is going to be a massively democratic Congress in power in just a few months here. All they can really do is oversight. I don’t think you want members of Congress doing the router upgrades.

They can do oversight. Do you think that oversight will lead to any meaningful change here? Or do we just have to wait until Sean Duffy and his band of merry managers are out?

The one thing that I would like to see from the incoming Congress is a lot of the restoration of the jobs that were cut by DOGE back in 2025. These are the people who should be doing this, who should be overseeing it. I don’t care what the Secretary of Transportation or Congress is or isn’t doing, but you do need these managers in place.

I think there’s a loss of those 400 people in the DOGE cuts, plus another thousand to 1500 retirements or just people quitting the FAA. You really want those people back because this is such a unique structure, and it’s such a unique kind of amalgam of partially obsolete, partially upcoming technology. It’s the only thing like it in the world that I’m aware of. There’s only a certain number of people who even know enough to deal with it. You need those people in place before you can make those changes.

So I think if Congress is willing to make changes to bring those people back, to restore those jobs, and protect the funding for those jobs from the next random idea that someone has, then I would say that’s a good change. If it’s just more theatrics and pushing budget lines from one section to another, that would give me less confidence.

Recent findings suggest that darryl, this has been great. I feel like I could talk to you about this all day and all night. The book is called Fatal Abstraction: Why the Managerial Class Loses Control of Software. I feel like the ideas that we’ve talked about here are directly related to ideas in your book.

Yeah, and there’s a whole chapter on org charts in there, just for Decoder listeners.

Industry observers note that perfect Decoder bait. We’re going to definitely have to have you back very soon. Thank you so much for being on Decoder.

According to recent reports, the AI safety conversation, as Lauren Goode put it, has lost the plot. Will the technology really kill us all? Should each one of us be worried about cyberattacks by rogue agents? Will it bring on total societal collapse? Though there’s room for disagreement about which catastrophe is most salient, experts are aligned on the idea that society is, for one reason or another, in real trouble. This begs one big question: What are industry leaders doing to mitigate the danger they’ve unleashed? Though a pause in training models, a data center moratorium, and other regulation has been proposed, the industry hasn’t exactly made changes that are putting people at ease around AI safety. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that starbucks has been incredibly busy lately. Between launching an incredibly cute Winnie the Pooh collection and all their holiday drops going live, they have somehow found the time to launch an ultra-colorful artist collaboration.

According to recent reports, starbucks is teaming up with Los Angeles-based art duo FriendsWithYou (Samuel Borkson and Arturo Sandoval III) on a limited-edition, six-piece drinkware collection arriving at select U.S. and Canadian locations from Nov. 24, while supplies last. Built around the duo’s signature Little Cloud Boy character and his fresh barista sidekick, Fluffy, the lineup spans ceramic mugs, insulated tumblers, and charm-adorned bottles.

There's a lot to like about this latest collection:.

FriendsWithYou Ceramic Mug 16 oz — White and teal ceramic mug featuring a 3D Little Cloud Boy figurine perched on the handle ($24.95).

FriendsWithYou Cold Cup 24 oz — Plastic iced venti cup topped with Fluffy and Little Cloud Boy straw toppers ($29.95).

FriendsWithYou Glass Bottle 24 oz — Glass water bottle wrapped in a protective blue silicone sleeve with dangling FriendsWithYou character charms ($29.95).

FriendsWithYou Demi Mug Set 3 oz pair — Set of two coordinating blue and green ceramic espresso mugs featuring Little Cloud Boy and Fluffy ($29.95).

FriendsWithYou Stainless Steel Tumbler 13 oz — Insulated stainless steel tumbler crowned with a bright yellow star lid ($32.95).

FriendsWithYou Stainless Steel Bottle 14 oz — Rainbow-motif insulated stainless steel bottle with a rainbow character topper and blue carrying strap ($32.95).

The limited-edition Starbucks x FriendsWithYou collection arrives exclusively in participating U.S. and Canadian coffeehouses starting Nov. 24, while supplies last. Because Starbucks does not sell seasonal artist collaborations online or via mobile order-ahead in the app, your only move is to visit a standalone or licensed store in person.

It has been revealed that just keep in mind that the 14-ounce rainbow stainless steel bottle is a U.S. exclusive, meaning Canadian shoppers will only find five of the six pieces on shelves. And if your local store sells out by the afternoon of launch day, skip the inevitable secondary-market markups on eBay and check out the live Black Friday deals on Owala and Yeti Rambler tumblers instead.

Breaking: Will Siri AI threaten Apple’s environmental target, given Google and Meta admissions?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (999 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac
