#2180. What is Sound Glow on HomePods, and how do you get it on your Apple speaker?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (678 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

What is Sound Glow on HomePods, and how do you get it on your Apple speaker?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple’s latest HomePod update makes the top of your speaker glow in sync with music.
  • Apple's HomePod has a basic set of lights on top that don't do much beyond glowing when Siri is listening or when something is playing.
  • HomePods don't have a traditional display like Apple's HomeView.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple’s latest HomePod update makes the top of your speaker glow in sync with music.

Apple's HomePod has a basic set of lights on top that don't do much beyond glowing when Siri is listening or when something is playing. But following the launch of the HomePod mini 2, Apple also introduced a upcoming feature called Sound Glow that makes better use of these lights. When turned on, the top of the speaker becomes a colorful light show synced to the song you're listening to — and the good news is that it's not exclusive to the latest HomePod mini. The feature is part of HomePod Software 27.2 and also works with the original HomePod mini and the HomePod 2 (the larger model). Here's a breakdown of how Sound Glow works and how you can enable (or disable) it on your HomePods.

HomePods don't have a traditional display like Apple's HomeView. Instead, Apple has included an array of LEDs on top along with a touch-sensitive surface that lets owners access quick controls such as volume and play/pause. With the latest HomePod software update, these LEDs are now used to make HomePods a little more fun with Sound Glow. Now, when you play a song, the speaker pulls colors from the album art and pulses them in time with the music's beat. Listening to Taylor Swift's The Life of a Showgirl will result in predominantly green and orange lights, while Miley Cyrus's Endless Summer Vacation will make the lights on your HomePod turn blue.

Recent findings suggest that apple indicates that the light animation reacts in real time to the bass and treble of the song being played, so two songs from the same album will glow differently. Also, Sound Glow isn't limited to songs — it also works with podcasts and Apple's ambient sounds. For instance, the Rain soundscape features an animation with a gentle pitter-patter effect. Songs without artwork or videos revert to the HomePod's standard white light. It all happens automatically and you really don't have to think about it.

It has been revealed that there are a few limitations worth noting, though. Don't expect Sound Glow to fully light up your living room — the lights aren't bright enough to do that unless the room is completely dark. The feature is also not available on the original HomePod released in 2018, even though it can be updated to the latest HomePod software. You'll also need an Apple Intelligence-enabled device paired with your HomePods for Sound Glow to work — that means an iPhone 15 Pro or newer, an M1 Mac or newer or one of the latest iPads. An Apple TV running tvOS 27 also does the trick to enable Sound Glow on your HomePods.

In a recent development, if you have HomePods and a compatible Apple device, setting up Sound Glow is easy, but you'll need to make sure they're all running the latest software first. That means HomePod Software 27.2 or later on your HomePods and iOS 27.2 on your iPhone or iPad. HomePods usually patch automatically after a while, but you can confirm in the Home app from another Apple device. Tap the three-dot button and select Home Settings, then look for the Software Update menu. Even a brand-upcoming HomePod mini 2 may need a software update, since it may ship with a version prior to 27.2 installed.

Once everything is up to date, you can finally enable Sound Glow. Go back to the Home app's main screen and tap your HomePod, then go to Settings and scroll down until you find the Sound Glow toggle. Just flip it on, and the feature will work — you'll need to do this for each HomePod individually. Ask Siri to play a song or use AirPlay on your iPhone to try out Sound Glow and see if it's working. And if you don't like Sound Glow, turning it off requires pretty much the same steps as turning it on, but now you'll have to flip the toggle to off instead.

Oregon and Virginia said the company broke state consumer protection laws.

The attorneys general of Oregon and Virginia have filed lawsuits against SpaceX Super Intelligence, accusing Elon Musk's conglomerate firm of violating state consumer protection laws by allowing users of its Grok AI chatbot to create non-consensual sexually explicit content. The lawsuit alleged that SpaceXSI released Grok's "spicy mode" as a way to "push its lagging product to tens of millions of latest users," which allowed for the creation of child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

Industry observers note that "This lawsuit is about seeking justice for the millions of Virginians who maintain accounts on X and were misled by the firm's false reassurances that their data and images would be safe on the platform," Jay Jones, Virginia's attorney general, remarked in a press release. "When xAI allowed Grok's creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it.".

This morning, X Safety posted that people using Grok for sexually explicit deepfakes "deliberately" violated the Terms of Service, adding that it will "keep testing and adjusting those protections as these abusers change tactics." X Safety also said that "protecting children is non-negotiable" and that CSAM "has no place on X or in Grok, and neither do explicit images of real people made without their consent.".

X Safety's post also said that the company would "take appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement," when users circumvent Grok's safeguards to create this type of content. Earlier this year, SpaceXSI filed a lawsuit against one of its users for creating sexual images of real people without their consent.

Sources indicate that beyond Oregon and Virginia, SpaceXSI faced several regulatory investigations and lawsuits in response to people generating illegal content. The City of Baltimore pursued legal action against Musk's manufacturer, claiming that Grok broke the city's Consumer Protection Ordinance; the UK's media authority and the California attorney general launched separate investigations into xAI and Grok.

Breaking: Jensen Huang Is Back as Nvidia CEO

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jensen Huang is stepping back into his role as chief executive of Nvidia effective immediately.
  • The stunning reversal comes 11 days after Huang resigned as CEO from the firm he cofounded 33 years ago, and after multiple declarations from the board of directors that it had no intention of reinstating him.
  • “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners, and customers,” said recently appointed board chair Harvey Jones in a press release announcing the decision.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang is stepping back into his role as chief executive of Nvidia effective immediately.

The stunning reversal comes 11 days after Huang resigned as CEO from the firm he cofounded 33 years ago, and after multiple declarations from the board of directors that it had no intention of reinstating him. On Monday, they took a conciliatory tone.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners, and customers,” said recently appointed board chair Harvey Jones in a press release announcing the decision.

Recent findings suggest that in that announcement the board noted it was “satisfied with respect to Mr Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia,” and that it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government” on the way to its decision. On Monday morning, President Donald Trump posted that the Nvidia board “has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO.”.

“I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” stated Huang in a statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”.

Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on November 12, and longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress was installed as his interim replacement. Five days later, Huang publicly announced that he was open to resuming his role as chief executive, noting the “outpouring of calls” from “employees, investors, business partners, and customers” advocating for his return.

“If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote.

The day Huang resigned, many Nvidia employees spoke up in his support. As reported by WIRED, employees left more than 1,600 comments on an internal “suggestion box” post in which they urged the company’s board to reinstall him as CEO.

It has been revealed that in the days following, a public petition calling for Huang’s reinstatement began circulating. At the time of writing, it has amassed more than 200,000 online signatures, the majority of whom self-identified as Nvidia shareholders. Tech elites like Elon Musk and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan have claimed that they were going to sign the petition or had signed it.

Huang’s reinstatement marks a total reversal from the public stance of Nvidia’s board of directors, which stated during the tech giant’s November 17 earnings call that it “does not intend” to reinstate him as CEO. WIRED has further reported that the board was alarmed by what one source described as Huang’s “lying” over the last year or so.

In a recent development, president Donald Trump, who developed a close working relationship with Huang during his second administration, had indicated openness to Huang returning as CEO. Trump told reporters on November 16 that he “would not mind” if Huang returned as chief executive, adding that he believed he had “learned a big lesson.”.

Huang’s resignation followed days of scrutiny over several extramarital romantic relationships: one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who has no known relation to Jensen, one with a Nvidia employee who directly reported to Huang, and one with a different Nvidia employee.

Huang’s relationship with Alice became the subject of particularly intense focus on November 6, when The Fresh York Times and Financial Times reported that US intelligence officials suspected that Alice may be an asset of the Chinese Ministry of State Security, both citing an intelligence briefing that circulated among top Trump administration officials last year. In the days since, some reports and Trump administration officials have questioned the accuracy of that intelligence. The Chinese government has consistently rejected claims that Alice was one of its spies.

According to recent reports, alice was the chief executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI company that’s been accused of helping Chinese tech companies use Nvidia’s most advanced chips at overseas locations, effectively sidestepping US export restrictions. Alice has also reportedly worked as a television reporter, at HSBC’s Hong Kong-based private banking arm, and at an investment bank backed by the Chinese state.

Sources indicate that huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, purportedly with the mission of bringing realistic 3D graphics to personal computers. For many years, the manufacturer was primarily known within the gaming community. It didn’t become a household name until the recent AI boom, when its graphic processing units (GPUs) became a crucial piece of infrastructure for powering advanced AI models.

Nvidia controlled about 90 percent of the global GPU market as of September 2026. The year prior, it became the first ever company to be valued at more than $4 trillion, though its stock price has been in precipitous decline since Huang’s resignation.

Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal, the companies confirmed Monday.

Crowdstrike and Zscaler said that the deal will create the “largest single addressable market” for cybersecurity, which will enable the companies to better position themselves for the AI era.

Zscaler is a San Jose, Calif.-based tech company that provides cloud cybersecurity products to about 8,000 enterprise companies. The company offers zero-trust technology, a security feature that requires employees to authenticate each and every time they access an internal system or resource. The aim is to protect against hackers from stealing credentials and using them to gain unfettered access to a company’s network.

Sources indicate that crowdStrike, which secures the computers, laptops, phones and other devices connected to a firm’s network, stated the deal will unite its endpoint protection software with Zscaler’s zero-trust platform to better defend their customers against data breaches. By combining the two products, CrowdStrike and Zscaler say that they can offer “superior protection” to their customers.

In remarks on Monday, the companies said that the acquisition will help customers safely adopt AI.

The deal, which is subject to regulatory approval, is expected to close around this time next year.

What the green flashing light on your Roku remote is telling you

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (692 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A remote that won't cooperate can put your streaming plans on hold.
  • Regardless of what you think of Fox's takeover, Roku is still an undeniable force in smart TVs.
  • Recent findings suggest that one of the reasons for the platform's popularity is its simplicity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A remote that won't cooperate can put your streaming plans on hold. Here's how to work out what's wrong and get back to the content you love.

Regardless of what you think of Fox's takeover, Roku is still an undeniable force in smart TVs. The manufacturer's products are an easy choice when looking for the best streaming devices, and of course a number of TVs now ship with Roku OS built in, most notably models from TCL and Hisense. Roku is the main game in town for brands that are not using Google TV, Fire TV or their own proprietary software.

Recent findings suggest that one of the reasons for the platform's popularity is its simplicity. That noted, there are times when the platform can be a little obtuse, mysterious blinking lights on the remote being a prime example. It's easy to assume that means a problem — but what, exactly?

Recent findings suggest that if you're dealing with a flashing green LED on your Roku remote, the fix could be very straightforward, simply requiring fresh batteries or a recharge, depending on the model. In some circumstances, however, you may need to do more or replace your remote entirely. Hopefully you've already got the Roku app on your phone as a backup, which can save you in a pinch when your remote is on the fritz.

As we just suggested, one reason for the light may be that your remote's batteries are low. If that's the case, swapping in fresh batteries (if there's no built-in one) should rapidly solve the problem. If you find this is happening too frequently, though, it may be because you're using rechargeable batteries. Alkalines are costlier in the long run — but Roku does recommend them for remotes with replaceable batteries. You can check battery levels in advance by navigating to Settings > Remotes & devices > Remotes > Your remote > About.

It has been revealed that you'll also see this light if you're trying to set up a replacement remote. Using your old one or the Roku app, you may need to head to Settings > Remotes & devices > Add devices > Remote > Continue to complete the process. You'll definitely see green flashing if you trigger a remote's physical pairing controls, which is done by holding a dedicated button or the Back and Home buttons simultaneously for five seconds.

Recent findings suggest that there's no need to be worried unless the light is flashing rapidly after re-pairing. If that's going on, it's a sign that your remote is probably broken and needs to be replaced. Note that you can also buy third-party remotes; sticking with one of Roku's official options should get you better support and features. Whatever you choose, verify that it's going to be compatible with your particular TV or streamer.

Industry observers note that if you've run through all of the above steps short of replacing your remote, one remaining option is to restart it. If it uses replaceable batteries, take them out, then press any two buttons before reinserting the batteries, negative sides first. If it uses a built-in battery, hold down its physical pairing controls (see the last section) for 20 seconds.

At this point, there's not much else you can try short of clearing the cache on your Roku or updating or rebooting your Roku device, or you could learn how to reset your Roku. Be warned that if you try a reset, you'll have to reconfigure everything as if it were right out of the box. It's also unlikely to solve a green light problem, since as we've established, that's normally related to battery levels or pairing, not buggy software.

If worst comes to worst, you may be stuck using your phone for control. One pro tip, though — you don't always have to use the Roku app. If your setup supports AirPlay from iPhone or MacBook to your TV or screen mirroring on Roku with your Android phone, you can often cut to the chase with whatever audio or video it is you're trying to play.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some apps really do need to know where you are, but plenty of others don't.
  • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
  • Industry observers note that when you download an app on a smartphone, you're usually prompted to agree to a list of permissions it needs to function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some apps really do need to know where you are, but plenty of others don't.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Industry observers note that when you download an app on a smartphone, you're usually prompted to agree to a list of permissions it needs to function. You may be asked to share your device's location when the app is open or grant unrestricted access in the background. Even website pop-ups halt your scrolling to ask for your location.

Industry observers note that it can be difficult to pick between staying in the dark and trading your location for services like maps, food deliveries and device tracking. Outside of those use cases, you may want to share your location from your iPhone with a friend or family member.

It has been revealed that today's devices have more safety features than they used to. Google, for instance, reviews Android apps that ask for background location access. But location data can be resold to third parties, so sharing it with apps and services you don't trust is risky. Here's how to weigh the pros and cons.

It has been revealed that staying connected makes your devices easier to find. While Find My is an easy smartphone anti-theft pick, sharing your location data with Apple AirTags and Tile trackers that work via Bluetooth lets you see your belongings in real time on a map. They can even play audio alerts, so you won't have to worry about losing your car keys inside your apartment again.

On a night out, people often share their location with friends for a sense of safety. Uber's Share My Trip feature lets you send your trip status and live location to up to five contacts. Snapchat's Snap Map, meanwhile, uses your location to track where you've made memories and find hotspots of activity to plan your next hangout. If you've set up the Personal Safety app on your Pixel phone, it can automatically call 911 and share your location if it detects a severe car crash.

According to recent reports, you can also share your location for a set time on your iPhone. iOS 26 lets you share for an hour, a day or indefinitely, and iOS 27 adds a custom option that runs from 15 minutes to 30 days. iOS 27 also lets you temporarily hide your location from people you normally share it with. On Android smartphones, Google's Find My Device app lets contacts share their location with you for a set duration as well. If you're meeting someone, you can also share your real-time location in Google Maps with an estimated time of arrival.

Sources indicate that sometimes you have no choice but to share your location data. Getting directions from Google Maps or Apple Maps, whether in a new city or on your home turf, requires letting the app see where you are. As a parent, you may want to see your children's location via services like Google Family Link. As a partner, maybe you shouldn't, even though many couples do. A Life360 survey of 1,000 US adults in relationships found that 95 percent use some form of location-sharing tech.

This can take a turn for the worse when personal safety is involved. Fitness-tracking apps like Strava store information on your jogging routines, revealing patterns that a stalker may use to deliberately run into you if you leave your information public. This goes for geotagged social media posts as well. Adding your location to a public Instagram Story might help your friends find you, but live updates like these may also draw attention from strangers.

In some cases, you may be able to get away with giving your location data momentarily or refusing altogether. Try not to hand out your location data to services that don't really need it to function. Delivery apps work just fine with manually entered addresses instead of being allowed to track your location. You can also use their browser-based versions to reduce the information you share.

Sources indicate that in 2022, Canadian privacy regulators found that Tim Horton's mobile app logged far more personal information than it had sought consent for, including detailed location data. As long as you're mindful of where your location data is being shared, you should be able to rely on the benefits of sharing while minimizing the odds of it falling into the wrong hands.

An unseen planet past Neptune may be in Earths weight class

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Math points to our solar system having another planet in Earth's weight class far beyond Neptune, tugging distant icy bodies onto strange orbits, a new study proposes.
  • Industry observers note that that would make it far smaller than Planet Nine, a hypothesized giant world five to 10 times Earth's mass that has drawn most of the attention in the hunt for an undiscovered planet.
  • "Imagine discovering, after decades of mapping our solar system, that another planet has been hiding from us all this time," said lead researcher Patryk Sofia Lykawka, of Kindai University in Japan, in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Math points to our solar system having another planet in Earth's weight class far beyond Neptune, tugging distant icy bodies onto strange orbits, a new study proposes.

Industry observers note that that would make it far smaller than Planet Nine, a hypothesized giant world five to 10 times Earth's mass that has drawn most of the attention in the hunt for an undiscovered planet. No one has spotted this suspected world, nicknamed Planet X2, but these researchers argue it would explain the strangest orbits in the outer solar system better.

"Imagine discovering, after decades of mapping our solar system, that another planet has been hiding from us all this time," said lead researcher Patryk Sofia Lykawka, of Kindai University in Japan, in a statement.

Every search for a missing planet has started the same way, with something in space that doesn't add up. In the 1800s, astronomers noticed Uranus wasn't staying on its predicted path, and the culprit turned out to be Neptune. Percival Lowell thought Uranus was still misbehaving and went looking for a "Planet X," a search that led to Pluto in 1930. But Pluto proved far too small to explain the trouble. Today, clues come from farther out, in a growing collection of frozen worlds beyond Neptune that move in ways the known planets can't explain. To many astronomers, that hints that something is still out there — maybe one planet, maybe more.

Beyond Neptune, a vast spill of icy leftovers from the solar system's birth circles the sun. Most of these objects travel in the Kuiper Belt, a broad band 38 to 50 times as far from the sun as Earth. Over the past 20 years, astronomers have found more and more of these objects on steeply tilted or stretched-out orbits.

In a recent development, in the new study, the researchers built a computer model of the young solar system. It included the four giant planets, thousands of small icy bodies, and 1,500 Pluto-size worlds. Then, the computer worked out how each body tugged on the others, step by step, across 4.5 billion years. When the team added Planet X2, up to twice Earth's mass, its gravity pulled some icy objects out of Neptune's reach and tipped others onto steep angles. Together, those effects reproduced the orbits of every known oddball, including Sedna, a distant world that swings far beyond the planets on a long, narrow loop. Models without the planet fell far short, according to the paper, published in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

Sources indicate that every hidden-planet study relies on computer models, but this one seems to replay more of the solar system's history. Early on, Neptune slowly drifted outward from the sun. As it moved, its gravity flung some icy objects far out and trapped others in orbits that march in step with Neptune.

Lykawka's own 2023 model skipped that drift and didn't include the main Kuiper Belt, where most known icy objects travel. It highlighted that Planet X2 could create the odd distant orbits, but not whether the planet would also wreck the parts of the belt that Neptune built. In the new model, Planet X2 creates the strange distant orbits and leaves the rest of the belt much like what astronomers see today.

A competing idea — that a few extra Mars- to Earth-size worlds formed among the giant planets and got flung around early on — fared worse in the team's model. The giant planets would have thrown those worlds out of the solar system within tens of millions of years — too fast to explain the strange orbits seen today.

Planet Nine faces problems of its own. Its backers proposed it after noticing that the orbits of a few distant icy objects seemed to point in roughly the same direction, as if something big had herded them into line. Other researchers have argued that the pattern may be a fluke, caused by having too few known objects and by telescopes watching only certain patches of sky. Several recently discovered distant objects follow orbits that don't fit what Planet Nine predicts, the authors say.

Sources indicate that in the researchers' best-fitting models, Planet X2 circles the sun at an average distance of about 33 billion to 46 billion miles. That's roughly 12 to 17 times as far out as Neptune, and nine to 13 times as far as Pluto. Even at its closest, the planet would stay nearly 19 billion miles from the sun — more than six times Neptune's distance. Its orbit would likely tilt only slightly from the path the other planets follow.

"If this planet exists, it could change how we understand the history of our solar system and how its most distant objects came to follow such unusual orbits," Lykawka remarked.

According to recent reports, the researchers admit the model doesn't fix everything. For example, compared with what a major sky survey found, the simulations predicted too few objects in the larger orbits the team studied.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which photographs the night sky again and again, could settle the debate, catching the planet as a faint, slowly moving dot. That's a tall order for something so far from the sun's light. Another possibility is that Rubin could find enough distant icy objects to show whether their orbits carry Planet X2's gravitational fingerprints.

"We now have an opportunity to put this idea to the test," noted study co-author Jonti Horner, a professor at the University of Southern Queensland, in a statement. "As the Rubin Observatory surveys the sky, we will find fresh clues that help us understand the distant reaches of the Solar System — and whether another planet is still waiting to be discovered.".

How to use AI glasses as a teleprompter

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you have the right type of smart glasses, this is an easy feature to enable.
  • In a recent development, out of all the myriad variations of smart glasses available today, the ones with built-in waveguides — such as the XGIMI MemoMind One and Even Realities G2 — have the most utility.
  • These glasses also have a built-in teleprompter mode that lets you deliver presentations or speeches while maintaining eye contact, and honestly, they're pretty good at it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you have the right type of smart glasses, this is an easy feature to enable.

In a recent development, out of all the myriad variations of smart glasses available today, the ones with built-in waveguides — such as the XGIMI MemoMind One and Even Realities G2 — have the most utility. Having a screen projected in your field of view that demonstrates notifications, turn-by-turn directions or real-time translations is particularly useful outdoors. The best part about using the MemoMind One and Even G2 is that these smart glasses don't have a camera, so there's no social stigma to using them outside.

These glasses also have a built-in teleprompter mode that lets you deliver presentations or speeches while maintaining eye contact, and honestly, they're pretty good at it. As the waveguides project the screen in your field-of-view, it feels natural to use glasses as a teleprompter. I tested the MemoMind One and Even Realities G2 with this mode, and here's what you need to know.

It has been revealed that the MemoMind One and Even G2 have a teleprompter feature that's easy to use; just load the script into the app, and you can select how fast (or slow) to scroll the text. Even's G2 reads PDF, plaintext, and DOCX files, but MemoMind One has just TXT and DOCX, with no PDF integration. This is mildly annoying if you regularly deal with PDF documents, but at least converting documents between file formats is trivial these days.

That remarked, MemoMind One has greater control over how you can view and control the teleprompter text. You can easily adjust font size, line width (which is a nice bonus), and adjust the display scaling just for the teleprompter. Both smart glasses have a nifty auto-follow feature that slows down or speeds up the text based on your speaking cadence. The feature (ostensibly) relies on AI to listen to your speech and adjusts the flow of the text accordingly. Other than that, you can get an auto-scroll option set to words per minute, and there's manual control as well.

It has been revealed that using the MemoMind One and Even G2 as a teleprompter is easy. I loaded up my Find X10 Pro Max review script and started talking, and the MicroLED-based waveguides did a good job projecting the text without otherwise inhibiting my field-of-view. You get to see the time elapsed (which is useful for me), along with battery level of the glasses and the current time. I don't routinely use a teleprompter, but having smart glasses to do so is far less of a hassle than setting up a dedicated one (at least in my use case).

Recent findings suggest that the waveguide prisms aren't that noticeable externally (unless someone is standing within 15cm of you), so if you're in a public setting, the text won't be visible to anyone in your vicinity. If anything, smart glasses are a good option in a public speaking setting as it gives you greater mobility — your teleprompter moves with you. Also, both the MemoMind One and Even G2 have monochrome waveguides with good brightness levels, and I didn't see any challenges making out the text while outdoors. I found the MemoMind One to get brighter than the G2 in outdoor use.

I've been using the Even G2 and MemoMind One interchangeably for most of the last six months. The G2 is a decent upgrade to the G1, and I like that the case has an integrated charger — that's one less cable for me to store. MemoMind doesn't do that, so I need to store the tiny dongle carefully so I don't lose the only way to charge the glasses.

According to recent reports, both glasses are lightweight at under 50g, and while the Even G2 is lighter, I found the MemoMind One to be more comfortable to wear. Battery life is better on the MemoMind One, and the glasses have onboard audio and sound tuned by Harman; they're great to listen to podcasts on the go. The G2 misses out on speakers altogether, so you don't get any built-in sound.

In a recent development, where the MemoMind One truly wins out is the control mechanism. The Even G2 uses a series of taps and swipe actions to control the glasses, with the gesture surface located at the temple tips, which is just awkward to use. There's also the small fact that it doesn't register gestures correctly at times, so I'm often scrolling or trying to trigger a gesture by reaching behind my ear, and it isn't the best look if you're in public.

Thankfully, the MemoMind One doesn't have these shortcomings; the glasses have a physical button located below the right hinge, and it's easy to interact. A single tap lets you cycle between menus, and a long-press action is used to exit to the dashboard. The UI wasn't quite as polished at launch, but MemoMind rolled out a slare of software updates over the last three months, and the glasses are on par with the Even G2 in this area.

Out of these smart glasses, I'd get the MemoMind One if I had to pick one. The MemoMind One just feels easier to wear, you can select three frame styles (G2 is limited to two), and it costs $499, $100 less than the G2. That's if you're getting the standard model; if you use prescription lenses, you'll need to pay an additional $280 for the MemoMind One and $159 for the Even G2. Of the two, the MemoMind One has the better feature-set as it has built-in audio and brighter waveguides, and I found it easier to wear and use.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps. Here are the details.

Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable owners to generate nonconsensual nude images.

According to the updated rules, apps that allow consumers to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.

Apple also warns that apps used primarily for pornographic content or the objectification of real people may be removed from the App Store without notice.

While definitely well-intended, Apple’s changes came amid growing reports of AI-powered nudify apps, which easily allow users to generate nonconsensual intimate images.

Two months before these changes, Apple removed an app that allowed customers to create pornographic deepfakes of real people after WIRED reached out for comment, which in turn came one month after San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu demanded that Apple and Google remove several nudify apps from their app stores.

Apple also removed several apps following investigations by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), which published reports in January and April revealing that such apps were widely available on the App Store, sometimes even appearing in sponsored search results.

Throughout these investigations, Apple has maintained that nudify apps have always been prohibited under its App Review Guidelines, and that it proactively rejects and removes apps that violate its policies, including those flagged through user reports.

Apple, of course, is not alone in this challenge, with Google facing similar criticism over their availability on the Play Store, and Meta coming under scrutiny for allowing developers to advertise these apps on Facebook and Instagram, as highlighted in the WIRED report mentioned above.

Which brings us to today’s report from The Guardian.

According to The Guardian’s exclusive report, “three Senate Democrats sent letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms.”.

A trio of US Senators say Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. They also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

The senators, namely Ron Wyden of Oregon, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Ben Luján of Latest Mexico, claim that in addition to failing to remove these apps, the companies may actually be profiting from their distribution and promotion.

Commenting on the letter, both Google and Meta stated they prohibit such apps or their promotion and work to detect and remove violations from their platforms, broadly echoing what Apple has repeatedly stated when reached for comment in the past over these same issues.

However, Wyden’s office argues that simply reaffirming, or in Apple’s case, updating these policies, means little if the companies continue to struggle to enforce them.

In a recent development, keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, said that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he added.

In its latest investigation, published just last month, TTP found 135 apps capable of generating nude or pornographic imagery on the App Store and the Play Store, using accounts registered to 13-year-old boys.

Additionally, researchers found that even accounts configured with parental controls were able to download these apps without requiring parental approval.

Despite Apple and Google removing the apps identified in the investigation, The Guardian noted that these apps continued to work on devices where they had already been installed.

Now, Senator Wyden warns that Congress may need to step in if the companies fail to do a better job of cracking down on these apps.

To read The Guardian’s full report, follow this link.

Recent findings suggest that upgrade, 8:40 p.m. ET: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple stated:.

“We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for people. A number of the apps in the TTP report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities. We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process — a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch. We previously removed 28 of the apps referenced in this report before it was shared with us and have taken action on the remaining apps found to violate our rules. The report also relies on testing from older software that does not reflect current Apple safety features, including expanded protections for teens and parental controls in Screen Time that give families the ability to block kids and teens from downloading apps rated above their age.”.

Expanding on the safety features mentioned in its statement, Apple noted that teens aged 13 through 17 now have certain protections enabled by default, including web content filters, even if their parents haven’t configured any restrictions, and pointed to ⁠this support article for more information.

The company added that children under 13 are required to use Child Accounts, and that the report relied on its previous 17+ age rating system, which was replaced last year with a more granular system that includes 13+, 16+, and 18+ ratings.

According to recent reports, just curious. Why doesn't someone from Apple try out the app before approving it, rather than approving it and waiting until people complain? I know there are many thousands of apps on the App store. But given that Apple makes money off most of these apps, it could surely afford to hire a staff charged with reviewing submitted apps to ensure compliance with the App store's guidelines and requirements before making them available in the App store. What am I missing here?

Apple also noted that in its report, TTP counted apps depicting people in swimwear or lingerie, which the firm said does not constitute nudification or, in itself, violate its guidelines.

It has been revealed that as for parental controls, Apple explained that, although apps that exceed a child’s configured age restrictions won’t appear in curated App Store sections, they can still be found through search, allowing children to request permission to download them through Ask to Buy. Without parental approval, the download remains blocked.

Apple added that Ask to Buy is supposed to require parental approval even for purchases made using gift card balances, including subscriptions. The firm stated that if a purchase didn’t trigger an approval request, that would be unexpected behavior, and that it is investigating further.

Patch, November 19, 4:00 p.m. ET: In response to Apple’s statement, TTP director Katie Paul reached out to 9to5Mac with the following comment:.

According to recent reports, apple’s statement on nudify apps sidesteps vital problems and leaves out key context. The company notes it prohibits nudify apps but doesn’t address how its age rating system for apps contributes to the problem. TTP has shown how Apple relies on information provided by app developers to set age ratings—a self-reporting system that allows many nudify and pornographic apps to be misleadingly labeled a suitable for minors. Apple also continues to talk about removing nudify apps from the App Store, without mentioning that apps that are “removed” continue to be fully functional on people’s phones.

Recent findings suggest that there are many questions about Apple’s policy on nudify apps that the statement fails to address. Apple has adopted a limited definition of “nudify.” The tech giant defines nudify apps as capable of showing someone naked, not stripping them down to a bikini or lingerie. But the company also indicates it bans “creepy” and “nonconsensual intimate imagery.” What if an app is used to depict a woman in a bikini without her consent? We have asked Apple to clarify that and have not heard back.

It has been revealed that as for Apple’s comment that TTP relied on “older software,” that may refer to the fact that Apple rolled out new child safety features in the fall. Our research was conducted in summer 2026. But many of Apple’s new features pertain to parent-supervised accounts on Apple, which have to be set up by a parent. Apple relies entirely on parents to go out of their way to locate and enable these settings. This raises obvious questions about how many people actually do this.

Today's NYT Strands hints will be easy if you have a short fuse.

Strands, the Newly introduced York Times' elevated word-search game, requires the player to perform a twist on the classic word search. Words can be made from linked letters — up, down, left, right, or diagonal, but words can also change direction, resulting in quirky shapes and patterns. Every single letter in the grid will be part of an answer. There's always a theme linking every solution, along with the "spangram," a special, word or phrase that sums up that day's theme, and spans the entire grid horizontally or vertically.

By providing an opaque hint and not providing the word list, Strands creates a brain-teasing game that takes a little longer to play than its other games, like Wordle and Connections.

Industry observers note that every once in a while, Instagram rolls out an update that addresses one of its users’ most longstanding requests. Today is one of those days.

As spotted by The Verge, Instagram head Adam Mosseri confirmed today that the app will finally let owners edit a Story after publishing.

This means users will be able to add stickers and drawings, fix typos or adjust text, and even change the music without having to delete the Story and publish it again, which would mean losing any views it had already received.

The catch is that people will only have 15 minutes after publishing a Story to make changes by tapping the ellipsis button at the bottom of the screen, and then selecting “Edit story.”.

Here’s Mosseri’s post announcing the news:.

A post shared by Adam Mosseri (@mosseri).

Today’s upgrade is the latest in a series of changes Instagram has made this year to address longstanding user requests.

Back in March, the app introduced the ability to reorder photos and videos in a carousel after publishing. In April, it added an option to edit comments (also within 15 minutes of posting), and in June, it began letting customers manually rearrange posts on their profile grid.

More recently, Instagram also brought its free Edits video editor to the Mac, with multi-track editing, advanced color grading tools, and 4K exports.

#2161. What is the best way to secure your PlayStation 5 for a flight?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

What is the best way to secure your PlayStation 5 for a flight?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, GTA 6 launches in November 2026, but unfortunately, you can't pause real life.
  • According to recent reports, the short answer is yes.
  • Sources indicate that this decision is ultimately up to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, GTA 6 launches in November 2026, but unfortunately, you can't pause real life. That business trip you had planned doesn't care about your other life in Vice City, so you'll have to get creative to keep playing while you're away from home. You might be asking yourself if you should just take your PlayStation 5 along with you, and frankly, nobody here is going to judge you for that. But is it even possible to carry a big, bulky gaming console with you on a plane?

According to recent reports, the short answer is yes. The TSA allows a PS5 in both carry-on and checked bags, but it recommends carry-on for fragile electronics. The only real problem with taking Sony's console along with you is the DualSense controller, which uses a lithium ion battery and needs some special care. The console itself just needs good padding. And if dragging your system through security sounds like too much for you, there is always the option of streaming remotely.

Sources indicate that this decision is ultimately up to you. Both the carry-on and checked-bag options present their own advantages and disadvantages. A carry-on means you'll have to, well, carry your PS5 with you the entire trip. That doesn't leave a lot of room for much else in your bag, but it also means you can keep an eye on your console at all times. Putting it in a checked bag frees up space for the flight, but with your system out of sight, you run the risk of an airport worker mishandling your luggage or losing it.

No matter your choice, packing your PS5 carefully matters. In a carry-on, make sure you wrap your console with a sweater or some other padding, and pack the cables with it. If possible, it's best to keep the carry-on under the seat in front of you to avoid all the shoving and shifting in the overhead compartments.

In a checked bag, the ideal way to pack your PS5 would be in the original box or inside a hard shell, but that isn't always realistic. As an alternative, place the console in the center of your luggage and completely surround it with soft clothes. If you have a hard plastic suitcase, that would be preferable to a soft-sided bag.

The DualSense controller has a lithium ion battery rated at 3.65 volts and 1,560 milliamp hours, which works out to about 5.7 watt hours. That is far below the 100 watt hour limit the FAA sets for lithium-ion batteries, so the controller is allowed on a plane. Still, the FAA indicates devices with lithium batteries should be carried in the cabin. If the controller has to be checked, it must be completely powered off and protected from damage or accidental activation. The reason is thermal runaway — a battery overheating and catching fire — which ULSE counted at an average of 2.36 incidents per week on passenger flights in 2025. In the cabin, flight crews are trained to recognize and respond to lithium battery fires.

It has been revealed that so keep your controller with you, make sure it is turned off or completely out of juice, and wrap it in some clothes or place it in a protective shell to keep it from getting damaged. Your best option would be an official DualSense carry case, like the one that comes with the DualSense Edge.

Industry observers note that there is a third option that allows you to keep playing from anywhere without having to carry your PS5 with you, and that is PlayStation's Remote play. This alternative allows you to stream your games online using your phone, a tablet or a laptop via your home console. Sony requires a connection of at least 5Mbps and recommends 15Mbps for a smoother picture.

For this to work, you need to keep your home console running in rest mode with "Stay Connected to the Internet" and "Enable Turning on PS5 from Network" activated. You can find these options under Settings > System > Power Saving > Features Available in Rest Mode.

Sources indicate that the PlayStation Portal makes this easier. It's a dedicated handheld that streams the PS5 over Wi-Fi. Sony says it works on public networks too, as long as it was first set up on the home network. Players with a PlayStation Plus Premium subscription can also use it to stream select games from Sony's servers with no console running at home.

Check the airline's carry-on size and weight limits against the console's dimensions.

Back up your save data and finish any pending updates.

Shut the console down completely, unplug everything, and take out the disc.

Wrap the power cable and HDMI cable, and pack them together with the console.

Pad the console in its original box, a hard case, or soft clothes toward the center of your luggage.

Switch the controller off and keep it in the cabin with you in a padded pouch.

At the hotel, make sure the TV has a free HDMI port before settling in.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that amazon shocked everyone in October when it introduced its new Alexa Tablet series with Google Play support built-in, addressing the biggest shortcoming of its older Fire Tablets. For Black Friday 2026, the Alexa Tablet 8 is a mere $150 and, with Google Play on board, this feels like a Fire Tablet that’s all grown up.

Industry observers note that the Alexa Tablet 8 is one of three latest Amazon tablets that rolled out in October with Google Play on board, and it’s also the one I was personally the most excited about. I love a good tiny Android tablet, but there just aren’t that many out there – and some of the ones we do have are exorbitantly expensive.

Right up there with Amazon’s long-running reputation in the tablet space, Alexa Tablet 8 is very much an affordable device, and that’s reflected in its fairly meager specs:.

Yet, I didn’t find myself put off by the device.

I specifically asked Amazon for a review unit of the absolute base model – 4GB of RAM and lockscreen ads – and I can say with confidence it’s Not Bad at the end of the day.

Recent findings suggest that the display is objectively not good, but it’s not really trying to be flashy either. The panel gets bright enough for most indoor use and, for general browsing or watching videos around the house or even on a flight, it gets the job done. If anything, my biggest complaint on the display was just how smudgey it gets with fingerprints.

It has been revealed that hardware is a strong suit. The Alexa Tablet 8 has an aluminum build that comes in this gorgeous teal color as well as a softer “Rosette” pink (or “Graphite,” if you want to keep it boring). It’s thin and light and slips into a bag easily, and even fit into the back pocket of my jeans. Buttons are clicky and aspects such as the speakers actually do well enough – like the display, the speakers aren’t good, but they’re not bad by any stretch either.

It has been revealed that amazon has a folio cover available that’s simple but nice, with a fabric finish that’s grippy. It’s an extra $40, though, which feels like a bit much for a super-affordable Android slate.

The biggest question was around the software experience, and this is where this upcoming effort really shines.

Alexa Tablet 8 ships with Android 16 out of the box, not FireOS or whatever Amazon was calling its forked experience on Fire Tablets (I genuinely refuse to go double-check because it’s a memory I’m thrilled to never have to revisit). It’s a pretty “stock” experience, with Amazon leaving aspects such as the notification shade/quick settings alone, and even the Settings menu feels pretty clean.

According to recent reports, that’s not to say nothing has changed. The homescreen has a fairly standard layout , but with these neat little corner widgets – one a “dynamic” widget with scrolling content (mostly ads) and the other a shortcut for Alexa search. Amazon is pushing Alexa as a voice assistant pretty heavily on these tablets, but I’m happy to report it’s pretty easy to ignore if you choose. These tablets will be great additions to your Alexa ecosystem if you’re invested, but I’m simply not.

The biggest change you’ll find is the lockscreen, where Amazon’s base models all come with lockscreen ads. This saves you about $20 on the hardware, and it’s not that bad of an experience. That stated, I’d absolutely spend the extra $20 at purchase to go without them, especially seeing as this blocks the ability to set a lockscreen wallpaper at all. It doesn’t cost anything more to remove them later, though, with a $20 charge through your Amazon account removing ads.

But what’s important here is that, for the fire time, Amazon is admitting defeat and installing the Google Play Store.

Industry observers note that alexa Tablet 8, and the rest of the lineup, has Google Play out of the box and access to any app you want. This means that you can, if you choose, fully ignore Amazon’s own services and do whatever you want. The smallest of examples: While Amazon’s built-in keyboard is fine, it’s wonderful that I don’t have to jump through hoops to switch over to Gboard. Fire Tablets were always an enticing value with a major catch, but Amazon’s change in this regard truly makes Alexa Tablets an attractive option for everyone – not just those willing to put up with the restriction or put in the work to hack Google apps on board.

It has been revealed that performance, despite the meager specs, is not awful. MediaTek’s low-end chip has just enough horsepower for general use, and 4GB of RAM isn’t as detrimental as I would have expected. It’s not fast by any means, but you could do a lot worse. There are 4GB Android tablets I’ve literally decided not to review because I couldn’t use them past the setup process, so the fact that Amazon is delivering a completely usable experience is a win in my book, even more so that I don’t actually mind using it. There’s a caveat to that, of course, and it’s that you shouldn’t expect to do a ton on this base model. For light browsing, reading Kindle books (or whatever other reading app since, you know, Google Play), or watching videos, this is great. For games, you’ll want to look elsewhere (and expect to spend more).

“Not awful” is kind of the pattern here.

Sources indicate that alexa Tablet 8 isn’t some shining example of a perfect budget tablet, but I think it really nails the fundamentals. At its usual $230~ starting price, it’s a plenty-good deal for those in the market for an affordable Android slate, but the Black Friday pricing of just $150 is all the better – I just wish the model with 8GB of RAM was also on sale.

Recent findings suggest that amazon’s pivot to Alexa Tablets is great – though I hope the manufacturer knows full well that everyone is still going to call these Fire Tablets or Kindles or whatever combination of brands that spring to mind. But that reputation might work in Amazon’s favor at the end of the day. While there’s a huge portion of the audience that’s been left frustrated for years at the lack of Play Store support on Fire Tablets, they’ve still been a market success for the most part, so this shift is just a win for everyone. Users get a better experience, Amazon gets to shuffle its priorities away from a dead app store, and the market as a whole gets an affordable piece of hardware that doesn’t suck.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The NYT Connections puzzle today is not too difficult if you have no sense of direction.

Industry observers note that connections is the one of the most popular New York Times word games that's captured the public's attention. The game is all about finding the "common threads between words." And just like Wordle, Connections resets after midnight and each new set of words gets trickier and trickier—so we've served up some hints and tips to get you over the hurdle.

According to recent reports, if you just want to be told today's puzzle, you can jump to the end of this article for today's Connections solution. But if you'd rather solve it yourself, keep reading for some clues, tips, and strategies to assist you.

In a recent development, the NYT's latest daily word game has become a social media hit. The Times credits associate puzzle editor Wyna Liu with helping to create the newly introduced word game and bringing it to the publications' Games section. Connections can be played on both web browsers and mobile devices and require players to group four words that share something in common.

Each puzzle features 16 words and each grouping of words is split into four categories. These sets could comprise of anything from book titles, software, country names, etc. Even though multiple words will seem like they fit together, there's only one correct answer.

If a player gets all four words in a set correct, those words are removed from the board. Guess wrong and it counts as a mistake—players get up to four mistakes until the game ends.

Players can also rearrange and shuffle the board to make spotting connections easier. Additionally, each group is color-coded with yellow being the easiest, followed by green, blue, and purple. Like Wordle, you can share the results with your friends on social media.

Zane Lowe shares Apple Music Radio audience numbers, recalls ‘crickets’ in the early days

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in a newly introduced interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month.
  • Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.
  • In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue stated Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in a newly introduced interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month. Here are the details.

Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.

In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue stated Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.

Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, however, has now offered a more concrete figure, revealing that the service reaches over 50 million unique listeners every month:.

According to recent reports, we were never, you know, delusional enough to assume we were going to get a huge audience overnight. We’d have to build it like anyone else would have to build anything. But we’ve just got to a point in our 11 years on where we now, overall, reach over 50 million unique listeners a month, which is a really large number for us, and it’s growing exponentially and really fast.

The revelation came in a wide-ranging interview published today with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, where Lowe discussed Apple Music Radio’s early struggles, its approach to supporting emerging artists, and why human curation remains central to the service.

When discussing the early days at Apple Music, Lowe recalled:.

When we started the radio here, I didn’t have access or opportunity with a lot of the artists that I built relationships with from the BBC because we were unproven. And I came over here thinking, “Well, I’ve got Jimmy Iovine over here, and I’ve got Apple over here and I feel unstoppable, and who’s not going to want to come and launch this thing with us?” But it was kind of crickets… As upsetting as that was at the time, two good things came out of it. Number one, it snapped me back into the reality force field of building something from scratch. And number two, it made us focus really clearly and in a major way on new and emerging artists.

He also mentioned some of the first artists Apple Music Radio supported, including Billie Eilish with “Ocean Eyes,” Khalid with American Teen, and Bryson Tiller with his first song.

At the time, Lowe noted, these artists were just getting started, and supporting emerging talent became a defining part of Apple Music Radio’s approach, one that continues to this day:.

The really cool number is on our radio network. We played — this year alone — over 6,500 individual artists, which is not a commercial radio model. [Other radio networks’] playlists are very small, and the amount of plays is very great. Our playlist is gigantic. We play a lot of different artists, and over half of those 6,500 artists we’ve played in one year are latest or emerging. So, think about 3,300 artists, roughly, getting played, who may be on their first song, their first EP, their first album…It’s proof of concept. It’s great.

Still on the subject of the early days at Apple Music, Lowe remarked “it was very clear [from the start] that that was very crucial to everybody who was responsible for bringing Apple Music to life,” adding that “serving artists and the artistic community in a way that is of most value and of most service” still drives “a lot of the decision-making” at the platform.

When the conversation turned to Apple Music’s recent rebranding, which introduced a newly introduced logo physically created using sound waves from a composition by Fred again.., Lowe said he couldn’t speak to the decisions behind it, but stressed the human element and the creative process that went into it:.

It has been revealed that we could have created that in a way that could utilize all of the tech available. We could type that into a prompt. But at the end of the day, seeing how it’s made is so much more additionally inspiring than just seeing it. It speaks to, I think, what we try to do here, which is, we love the process of what we do, and the result is a byproduct of getting to do it and loving to do it.

The issue of algorithms also came up when Lowe discussed Apple Music’s approach to music discovery, with the executive emphasizing the importance of human curation over automated recommendations:.

According to recent reports, well, we don’t want to say that too loudly, because someone could be like, “Wait a minute, we could cut costs here? Man, how did we not think of that!” Look, I mean, jokes aside, we’ve been incredibly fortunate, and I’ve been incredibly fortunate to take that step from the BBC into a company and to work with people that value exactly what it is you’re describing: this idea of place and this experience of sharing things with each other, and how meaningful it is when someone shares a record with you and it comes with context. It’s a gift….

#2156. Public vs. private IP addresses: what's the difference?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (694 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Public vs. private IP addresses: what's the difference?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (694 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One identifies your network, the other identifies the devices using your network.
  • In a recent development, each time you stream a video, read an article or download files online, your network interface and a server communicate with each other using unique numerical labels called IP addresses.
  • All the various gadgets connected to your home home network like phones, computers and smart home hardware connect to your router via private IP addresses rather than the public address assigned to your router.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One identifies your network, the other identifies the devices using your network.

In a recent development, each time you stream a video, read an article or download files online, your network interface and a server communicate with each other using unique numerical labels called IP addresses. When you acquire an internet connection, your ISP assigns a unique public IP address to your router's WAN port. The public IP address is what allows you to access the internet and the internet to find you.

All the various gadgets connected to your home home network like phones, computers and smart home hardware connect to your router via private IP addresses rather than the public address assigned to your router. Devices on private IP addresses can communicate with each other but cannot directly access the internet; they must rely on a router. Similarly, devices outside the private network cannot communicate with those using a private IP address. This is why your neighbor cannot send a print request to your home printer.

Industry observers note that when attempting to understand public vs. private IP address, you can think of the former as your house address and the latter as apartment numbers. Each device connected to your router is assigned a unique private IP address. Knowing how to find the IP addresses of your connected devices can help streamline troubleshooting efforts in case your home network starts acting up.

The quickest way to find your public IP address is via an online IP checker tool like WhatIsMyIPAddress and ifconfig.me. You can use any device connected to your router for this process as long as it's capable of accessing a web browser. To identify private IP addresses, you can use your router's control panel to view the list of devices connected to your home network, including their private IP addresses. However, this method may not be sufficient to identify which IP address corresponds to what device as not all device manufacturers include hostnames.

Sources indicate that in case a device's hostname doesn't show up in your router's control panel, you're not entirely out of options. For instance, on a Windows computer, you can run the "ipconfig" command to find the IPv4 address, which is the computer's private IP address. On macOS, running the "ipconfig getifaddr en0" (Wi-Fi) or "ipconfig getifaddr en1" (ethernet) commands will pull up the computer's private IP address.

Sources indicate that on an iPhone: Settings > Wi-Fi > tap the "i" button next to Wi-Fi network you're connected to > scroll down to find the IPv4 section containing your iPhone's private IP address. Similarly, on an Android device: Settings > Network and internet > Internet > tap the network you're connected to > scroll down to find your device's private IP address.

Your public IP address identifies your network on the internet while your private IP addresses identify devices connected to your home network. Although each device in your home network has its own private IP address, your router allows them to share a single public IP address when accessing the internet. This is made possible via Network Address Translation (NAT), which is a network routing mechanism that enables the router to manage communication between devices in your private network and the internet.

While home networks are usually assigned a private IP address that follows the 192.168.X.X IP DNS range, the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) has also reserved the 10.X.X.X and 172.16.X.X private IP ranges for large and medium organizations, respectively.

Learning how to recognize public and private IP addresses can help you identify devices in your home network and troubleshoot connectivity issues effectively. For instance, if a device in your network has an unusual 169.254.X.X IP address, also known as Automatic Private IP, instead of the familiar 192.168.X.X IP range, you can conclude that the device did not receive the IP address from the router. In case devices in your home network do have valid private IP addresses but no access to the internet, you can then focus your investigation on the most probable cause — your router, followed by the ISP — rather than troubleshooting everything in the network chain.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s been a wild ride for Google Pixel’s App Lock feature, but the company is officially re-releasing the feature today, right alongside its debut on Samsung Galaxy devices.
  • App Lock debuted on Google Pixel in an August build of Android 17 QPR2’s beta.
  • The feature is still only in Android 17 QPR3 Beta 3 for Google Pixel devices, an update that should be released to the stable track in early 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been a wild ride for Google Pixel’s App Lock feature, but the company is officially re-releasing the feature today, right alongside its debut on Samsung Galaxy devices.

App Lock debuted on Google Pixel in an August build of Android 17 QPR2’s beta. The feature lets customers hide apps behind a biometric or PIN authentication layer while also hiding notifications, widgets, and data from AI services. It’s a useful privacy features, but one that Google removed in subsequent updates. The feature later returned in QPR3 Beta 3 last month, and today Google is officially re-releasing it.

The feature is still only in Android 17 QPR3 Beta 3 for Google Pixel devices, an update that should be released to the stable track in early 2027.

Sources indicate that pixel owners on stable Android 17 QPR2 should already have this! Why would Google make Pixel owners wait until March 2027 to get this?! Release it now to Pixel owners. 🤨.

You can still access App Lock by long-pressing on an app icon and adding it to the app lock list.

In a post on Reddit, Google’s Community Engagement Manager details that App Lock on Google Pixel was removed for improvements before getting a full release:.

…the product team decided to temporarily pull back the feature from the QPR2 Beta to allow for additional polish, thorough testing, and robust integration across all system surfaces.

That’s why Samsung’s One UI 9.5 beta release today also brings support for App Lock. The feature is built into Android 17 QPR2, seemingly the release that One UI 9.5 is based on, but Google Pixel devices aren’t getting it until QPR3. As far as release timelines go, this means that Samsung’s Galaxy S27 series will probably ship with this feature out of the box, where Pixel phones won’t get it until around March or so. One UI 9.5 won’t roll out for older Galaxy devices until May, if One UI 8.5 serves as an example.
